The findings highlight a time-limited treatment effect beyond an early placebo response and require further investigation of LDRT as a conservative, non-pharmacological option for selected patients. Trial registration: clinicaltrials.gov NCT05562271.

title: Intratumoral microbiota heterogeneity and Bifidobacterium abundance are linked to very early recurrence in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Although intratumoral bacteria have been reported in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the compositional differences between HCC and adjacent non-tumor tissues remain controversial, and the specific taxa correlated with very early postoperative recurrence remain unexplored. We collected tumor and paired normal tissues from 131 HCC cases for 16 S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing. Multiple bioinformatics approaches compared microbial composition, diversity, and enriched taxa between tumor and normal tissues. Intratumoral microbiota was also compared between HCC patients with very early recurrence (VER) and those without VER. HCC tissues with high versus low Bifidobacterium abundance underwent transcriptomic sequencing to identify differentially expressed genes and pathways, with immune cell profiling. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL), and immunohistochemistry evaluated the association between Bifidobacterium presence/abundance and apoptotic signaling pathways, as well as apoptosis-related marker proteins. Microbial diversity did not differ between HCC and normal tissues, but compositional differences and inter‑individual heterogeneity were evident. Bacterial composition overlapped substantially among tumor tissue, adjacent tissue, and bile across taxonomic levels. Intratumoral Bifidobacterium abundance was significantly lower in VER patients than in non-VER patients. FISH confirmed intratumoral Bifidobacterium . Bifidobacterium enrichment correlated with enhanced apoptotic activity, reduced baculoviral IAP repeat containing 5 (BIRC5) expression, and consistent TUNEL and cleaved caspase‑3 staining. Reduced intratumoral Bifidobacterium abundance is linked to very early postoperative recurrence of HCC, though this finding needs validation in multi‑center cohorts.

title: Longitudinal associations between loneliness and outcomes of Common Mental Disorders (CMDs): A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Loneliness has been increasingly associated with poor mental health outcomes, yet its prognostic role in people with Common Mental Disorders (CMDs) remains unclear. This systematic review aimed to examine whether loneliness is longitudinally associated with mental health outcomes in individuals with CMDs, regardless of treatment status. Methods We searched PsycINFO, MEDLINE, Embase and CINAHL from inception to October 2025 for longitudinal studies examining associations between baseline loneliness and CMD outcomes at follow-up. Eligible studies included adults aged 16+ with CMDs. We conducted a narrative synthesis and where appropriate, random-effects meta-analyses for binary depression outcomes reflecting unfavourable course (recurrence, persistence, or non-remission). Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42023410401). Results We included 22 studies, of which the majority focused on depression-related outcomes (operationalised as symptom severity, recurrence, persistence, remission, and service utilisation). Our narrative synthesis showed consistent associations between higher baseline loneliness and poorer depression-related outcomes at follow-up in people with CMDs across clinical, community, and treatment settings. Meta-analysis of four studies (all in older adults with depression) showed that individuals reporting loneliness at baseline had over three times the odds of poor depression outcomes at follow-up compared with those not lonely (pooled adjusted OR 3.26, 95% CI [2.26–4.70], p < 0.001). This finding should be interpreted with caution, as only one of the four studies adjusted for baseline depressive symptom severity. The few studies capturing suicidal ideation, anxiety, and mixed CMD outcomes found limited and inconsistent evidence. The GRADE certainty of evidence was high for depression outcomes, low for suicidal ideation and anxiety outcomes, and very low for mixed CMD outcomes. Conclusions Loneliness is consistently associated with poorer subsequent depression outcomes in people with CMDs, particularly depressive disorders. These findings suggest loneliness may represent an important prognostic factor in depression and warrant further evaluation in intervention studies. Further high-quality longitudinal research is needed to clarify whether—and under what conditions—loneliness affects outcomes for other CMDs and treatment effectiveness.

title: Artificial intelligence-based assessment of gastric mucosal exposure and its association with lesion detection: a multicenter study
abstract: Completely and clearly visualizing the mucosa during esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) improves high-risk lesion detection. Here we propose a new EGD quality control indicator and present the optimal gastric mucosal exposure area (OGMEA) system to automatically assess mucosal exposure and examine its association with the detection of early gastric cancer and other gastric lesions. A segmentation model was developed to assess mucosal exposure. Expert endoscopists defined a standard for 19 gastric anatomical sites. Images exceeding the OGMEA threshold were considered adequately-exposed. The OGMEA was validated using a multi-center dataset from a randomized controlled trial involving 25,320 participants from 24 centers. Associations between OGMEA and lesion detection were assessed at the anatomical-site and patient levels. Patient-level associations were evaluated using center-clustered multivariable logistic generalized estimating equation models adjusted for trial allocation, the number of screened standard anatomical sites, and inspection time. Of assessed sites, 46.36% and 53.64% were adequately and inadequately exposed, respectively. Detection rates of EGC, gastric neoplasms, precancerous conditions, and focal lesions were significantly higher in adequately-exposed sites than in inadequately-exposed sites ( P <0.001). At the patient level, the number of adequately-exposed sites was positively correlated with lesion detection across all lesion categories (ρ = 0.830-1.000, all P <0.01). In adjusted analyses, each additional adequately exposed site was associated with higher odds of detecting EGC (aOR 1.081, 95% CI 1.021–1.146, P = 0.008), precancerous conditions (aOR 1.056, 95% CI 1.017–1.096, P = 0.004), and focal lesions (aOR 1.059, 95% CI 1.006–1.114, P = 0.028). The association with neoplastic lesions was similar in direction but did not reach statistical significance (aOR 1.038, 95% CI 0.998–1.080; P = 0.060). Effect estimates were materially consistent in endoscopist-clustered sensitivity analyses. OGMEA may serve as a practical quality indicator for EGD, with greater mucosal exposure associated with higher lesion detection.

title: Determinants of failure of midazolam monotherapy during continuous deep sedation until death: evidence from a French cohort in a palliative care unit
abstract: Abstract Background Continuous deep sedation until death (CDSUD) is a legally regulated practice in France relying primarily on midazolam as first-line therapy. However, additional sedative agents are frequently required, and determinants of failure of midazolam monotherapy remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify factors associated with failure of midazolam monotherapy during CDSUD, defined as the need for second- or third-line sedative agents. Methods We conducted a retrospective single-centre observational study including all patients undergoing CDSUD in a university hospital palliative care unit between 2020 and 2024. Demographic, clinical, pharmacological, and organisational data were collected. Associations with failure of midazolam monotherapy were assessed using univariable and multivariable logistic regression. Age was modelled using restricted cubic splines to account for non-linear effects. Results Among 1,376 patients admitted to the unit, 287 underwent CDSUD with midazolam as first-line treatment. Median age was 69 years (IQR 59–77), and 52.3% were male. Cancer was the main diagnosis (74.2%). Failure of midazolam monotherapy occurred in 211/287 patients (73.5%). Among these patients, escalation consisted of chlorpromazine alone in 134/211 patients (63.5%), propofol alone in 20/211 patients (9.5%), and both agents in 57/211 patients (27%). In multivariable analysis, polypharmacy was independently associated with an increased risk of failure of midazolam monotherapy ( P= .002), both in patients receiving 5–9 medications (OR 3.06, 95% CI 1.60–5.91) and in those receiving ≥ 10 medications (OR 3.05, 95% CI 1.22–8.11). Sedation performed in the context of withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment was also associated with failure of midazolam monotherapy (OR 3.51, 95% CI 1.46–9.88). Age showed a significant non-linear association with outcome ( P <.001). Oxygen therapy within the 24 h preceding sedation induction was associated with a reduced risk of failure (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.65). Conclusions Failure of midazolam monotherapy during CDSUD is common and associated with polypharmacy, and specific clinical contexts. The non-linear effect of age highlights complex pharmacological responses at end of life. These findings support individualized sedation strategies and early anticipation of combination therapy.

title: Non-cancer multimorbidity in people diagnosed and living with and beyond cancer: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Multimorbidity is common at cancer diagnosis, and both cancer and its treatment can lead to new long-term conditions. However, evidence on the prevalence of multimorbidity, particularly mental-physical multimorbidity, at both diagnosis and five years after cancer diagnosis remains limited. This study describes the prevalence of, and factors associated with, non-cancer multimorbidity in people newly diagnosed with cancer and those living with and beyond cancer. Methods Retrospective cohort study of people aged 18 years and older diagnosed with, or surviving five years with one of breast, prostate, colorectal or lung cancer in 2018. For 46 long-term conditions, multimorbidity (≥ 2 non-cancer conditions), mental-physical multimorbidity (≥ 1 non-cancer physical and ≥ 1 mental health condition) and condition count (0 - ≥6 non-cancer conditions) were measured in incident and survivor cohorts, and examined by age, sex, deprivation and ethnicity. Odds of multimorbidity by cancer type was calculated using logistic regression, stratified by sex and adjusted for age, deprivation and ethnicity. Results Analysis included 33,258 people with incident cancer and 16,807 people living with and beyond cancer (PLWBC). Multimorbidity ranged from 60 to 86% at cancer diagnosis to 70–90% in PLWBC, dependent on cancer type. Less than 20% had no additional long-term conditions at diagnosis (< 5.3% in lung cancer specifically) and less than 15% in PLWBC (< 2.3% in lung cancer). Mental-physical multimorbidity affected 24–39% at diagnosis and 27–44% in PLWBC. Both types of multimorbidity were higher in those living in the most deprived areas across all age groups. Compared with colorectal cancer, people with lung cancer had higher odds of multimorbidity at both diagnosis (in women adjusted OR 2.15 95%CI 1.86–2.49; in men aOR 1.71 95%CI 1.50–1.94) and in PLWBC (in women aOR 2.11 95%CI 1.45–3.12; in men, aOR 2.20 95%CI 1.51–3.30), whereas women with breast cancer and men with prostate cancer had lower odds. Conclusions Most people with cancer have additional long-term conditions, with the highest prevalence in lung cancer. Clear socioeconomic inequalities in multimorbidity persist into survivorship. Cancer pathways need to ensure coordinated management of non-cancer long-term conditions between primary and secondary care across the whole cancer journey, from diagnosis through treatment and into survivorship.

title: Targeting food addiction through an intensive energy-reduced Mediterranean diet lifestyle intervention: evidence from the 3-year PREDIMED-plus trial
abstract: Food addiction (FA) has been proposed as a behavioural phenotype linked to obesity, potentially influencing adherence and response to lifestyle interventions. Its role within long-term, multicomponent weight-loss programmes remains unclear. This study evaluated the impact of an intensive lifestyle intervention based on an energy-reduced Mediterranean diet (MedDiet) on FA symptomatology and examined whether baseline FA predicts adherence and weight-loss outcomes. A total of 448 older adults (mean age = 65.3 ± 4.6 years) with overweight/obesity and metabolic syndrome from the PREDIMED-Plus Cognition sub-study were randomised to an intensive intervention (IIG; energy-reduced MedDiet, physical activity, behavioural support) or a control group (CG; ad libitum MedDiet). FA (measured using the Yale Food Addiction Scale 2.0), anthropometric measures, MedDiet and physical activity adherence, and quality of life (QoL) were assessed at baseline, 1- and 3-years follow-up. Longitudinal changes were analysed using repeated-measures ANOVA. Logistic and Cox regression models evaluated predictors and time-to-achievement of clinically meaningful outcomes. Structural equation modelling (SEM) explored 3-year pathways linking anthropometric measures, MedDiet adherence, QoL, and intervention group according to FA status. FA severity decreased in both groups, but reductions were sustained only in the IIG, which showed lower FA scores than the CG at 3 years ( p = 0.011). The IIG increased the likelihood of achieving clinically meaningful reductions in weight and waist circumference, particularly among participants without FA at baseline (≥ 8% weight loss: OR = 2.87, 95%CI 1.99–4.14; ≥5% waist circumference reduction: OR = 3.01, 95%CI 2.20–4.11). Improvements in MedDiet adherence were markedly greater in the IIG, with effects strongest among individuals without FA (OR = 5.82, p < 0.001). SEM indicated that adherence mediated long-term improvements in weight, waist circumference, and QoL only in individuals without FA. An intensive energy-reduced MedDiet-based intervention improves FA symptoms and cardiometabolic outcomes. However, baseline FA appears to limit adherence and attenuates long-term benefits. FA may represent a clinically relevant phenotype for personalising obesity treatment and enhancing intervention effectiveness. International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN): 89,898,870. Registration date: 24 July 2014.

title: Implementing reproductive carrier screening to include diverse Asian populations: insights from Singapore
abstract: Abstract Background As part of Singapore’s effort towards precision medicine tailored to Asian diversity, we describe the implementation of a nationwide reproductive carrier screening program. Using a customised 112-gene panel, targeting population-specific recessive genetic diseases, we outline the overall program design, and initial efforts of community and stakeholder engagement to inform culturally appropriate implementation. Methods Participants receive culturally tailored online education regarding our reproductive screening program and are provided results with genetic counselling and reproductive options. Engagement with religious leaders indicated support for the program. Community and stakeholder perspectives were assessed through questionnaires. Results Recruitment is nation-wide, and since initiation of our pilot phase in September 2024, 1,619 couples have registered interest, with 60% uptake of those deemed eligible. Among the 550 couples that have received results to date, six couples (1.0%) were identified to be at increased risk. Community questionnaire responses ( n = 1,002), involving couples who participated in the program as well as the general public, indicated interest was high (59%) across the cohort but awareness, intent to participate and implications for reproductive options differed by sociodemographic factors such as ancestry and religion. Healthcare professional respondents ( n = 113) acknowledged carrier screening will be routine in medical care, but report limited confidence and resources. Conclusions These early program outcomes and community engagement are guiding the implementation of expanding population-based carrier screening in Singapore, contingent on addressing practical challenges through equitable outreach and professional training.

title: Incidence and predictors of delirium-associated violence towards healthcare workers in a Swiss ICU: results from the CAVE study
abstract: Abstract Background To assess the frequency of delirium coinciding with aggressive and/or violent patient behavior in intensive care unit (ICU) patients as documented by nurses and to identify clinical associations or risk factors. Methods This was a retrospective observational cohort study conducted at University Hospital Basel in Switzerland including data from 2023-2024. Data collected included demographics, treatment characteristics, clinical scores (including the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Score [RASS] and the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist [ICDSC]) and interventions. The primary objective was to assess the prevalence of delirium in patients with aggressive/violent behavior within ±72 hours of incidents. Secondary objectives included identifying independent associations with violence via uni- and multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 10,817 ICU patients, 300 (2.8%) were reportedly aggressive or violent. Delirium occurred in 89.3% of patients within 72 hours of the event and 76.7% were delirious at event. Violence was mostly physical (80.4%), with 22.2% preceded by aggression within a median of 21.6 hours. Multivariable analyses identified an increasing RASS (OR = 1.46 per increasing unit ; p = 0.001) and ICDSC (OR = 1.14 per increasing unit ; p = 0.039) before the violent incident as independent associations. Management shifted from verbal de-escalation for aggression to more invasive measures for violence; sedation rose from 45.3% to 69.8% (p < 0.001), restraint use from 20.0% to 43.1% (p < 0.001) and sedation-related complications reached 64.9%. Unchanged one-on-one nursing rates indicate a reliance on restrictive measures over staffing increases. Conclusions While ICU-related aggression and violence is rarely reported, the independent association of increasing RASS/ICDSC scores before violence and a prodromal phase of aggression in many cases provide a warning pattern. Identifying these early signs could allow for proactive de-escalating intervention, potentially reducing the need for physical restraints and heavy sedation.

title: Time-to-expiration for evidence bodies of medication harms (TIME): survival analysis from a retrospective cohort
abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are cornerstones of evidence-based medicine, yet their conclusions can be revised or overturned as new evidence emerges. Prior research has mapped how systematic‑review conclusions evolve, but no empirical study has quantified how evidence on drug harms shifts over time. We aimed to examine the stability of safety evidence. We conducted a before‑and‑after comparison study using the SMART Safety dataset, a well-established empirical resource for evidence synthesis of medication-related harms. For each eligible meta‑analysis, we aggregated trial‑level 2 × 2 data annually and applied the IVhet model to generate cumulative effect estimates over time; Kaplan–Meier survival analysis was applied to estimate time to signals of evidence expiration and convergence, with the first-year cumulative estimate as the starting point. We defined signals of evidence expiration as the first change in effect direction, statistical significance, or a ≥ 50% relative change in the pooled odds ratio (OR), and convergence as a ≤ 0.10 absolute difference between consecutive cumulative ORs over five annual iterations. Median times to expiration and convergence were then estimated across eligible meta‑analyses. We included 505 meta-analyses, spanning 310 harm outcomes, with a median of 328 adverse events per meta-analysis. During follow-up, signals of evidence expiration occurred in 356 (70.5%) of these early-stage evidence, with a median time of 3 years (95% CI 3 to 4). Among expiration events, 117 (32.9%) were triggered solely by a ≥ 50% relative change in effect magnitude, and 89 (25.0%) met two or three criteria simultaneously. Subgroup analyses showed similar patterns, with medians ranging from 2 to 7 years. For the 416 with I² < 50%, 278 (66.8%) met the expiration definition, with a median of 4 years (95% CI 3 to 4). Only 27 early-stage evidence (5.3%) met the convergence criterion during follow‑up; the 5th and 25th percentiles for time to convergence were 9 and 31 years, respectively, while the median was not estimable. Current evidence suggests that early meta‑analytic evidence on harms may expire within a relatively short time, while signals of convergence tend to appear much later. These observations point to cautious interpretation of meta‑analytic evidence on harms and suggest that timely updating should be considered.

title: Safety, efficacy, and biomarker analysis of HTMC0435 plus temozolomide in relapsed extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer: A phase Ib/II trial
abstract: Second-line treatment options for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) are limited. This study investigated HTMC0435, an oral Poly-ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, combined with temozolomide in patients with relapsed ES-SCLC. In this phase Ⅰb/II trial (NCT05728619), patients with relapsed ES-SCLC who had been treated with one or two lines of previous therapy received HTMC0435 plus temozolomide until disease progression or intolerable toxicity. The recommended phase II dose (RP2D) of HTMC0435 was determined per results from the phase Ib part with a “3 + 3” dose-escalation design, while temozolomide was given at a fixed dose of 75 mg/m 2 on days 1–7 of each 21-day cycle. The primary endpoints were dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), maximum tolerated dose (MTD), RP2D, and adverse events. From February 2023 to November 2023, a total of 59 patients were enrolled. As no DLT occurred in the phase Ib part, the MTD could not be determined in this study. Fifty-five patients (three in phase Ib and 52 in phase II) received HTMC0435 at RP2D (8 mg twice daily). Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 33 (55.9%) of 59 patients, with the most common being neutropenia (23 [39.0%]) and leukopenia (18 [30.5%]). No treatment-related deaths occurred. Efficacy was evaluable in 48 patients, with an objective response rate of 25.0% (12/48; 95% CI: 13.6–39.6). Median overall survival in all the 55 patients was 11.2 months (95% CI: 8.97–13.14). Similar benefit trends were observed between platinum-sensitive (chemotherapy-free interval ≥ 90 days) and platinum-resistant (chemotherapy-free interval < 90 days) patients. HTMC0435 plus temozolomide showed a manageable safety profile and initial indications of anti-tumor activity in patients with recurrent ES-SCLC, but further validation is needed in randomized controlled trials.

title: Effects of neuromodulation techniques on neuropathic pain: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
abstract: Although neuromodulation is widely used for neuropathic pain (NP), high-quality comparative evidence on the analgesic effects of different techniques is lacking for most NP subtypes, except for well-defined conditions such as complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS). This gap leaves clinicians with limited guidance on optimal technique selection in most clinical scenarios. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus were systematically searched from inception to July 1, 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) employing neuromodulation techniques for the treatment of NP were included. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was used to assess bias. Network meta-analysis was based on Bayesian models and implemented in R 4.2.3 and Stata. The Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) program is based on the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system to evaluate the level of evidence in the results. The conclusions are based on the evidence from the network meta-analysis (NMA) using a partially contextualised framework. 115 RCTs evaluating 19 neuromodulations were included. LF-SCS was identified as the neuromodulation with substantial evidence for neuropathic pain, supported by moderate certainty. PNS, HF-SCS, RFT, DRGS, b-PRF, and Hv-PRF showed favorable analgesic effects, although the certainty of evidence was low. Non-invasive transcranial neuromodulation techniques demonstrated limited analgesic benefits with low certainty evidence, suggesting that further studies are needed. Overall, this review provides a comparative overview of the efficacy and evidence certainty of various neuromodulation techniques, offering a basis for future research and clinical decision-making.

title: Bayesian probabilistic statements for communicating clinical trial results
abstract: Abstract Background Clinical trials are often analyzed using frequentist methods and results are interpreted according to their statistical significance. However, p-values and effect measures such as odds or hazard ratios are poorly understood by researchers and policymakers, and even less by patients and clinicians. Moreover, communicating uncertainty around treatment effects is challenging. Probabilistic statements from Bayesian analyses (e.g., the probability that a drug is more effective than placebo) offer an intuitive way to convey results and uncertainty, may provide insight, and support clinical decision-making. We aimed to (i) empirically evaluate the utility of probabilistic statements by re-analyzing data from previously published trials using Bayesian methods, and (ii) provide instructional examples of how probabilistic statements can be used to communicate and interpret results from clinical trials. Methods We analyzed data on primary outcomes obtained from trials previously published in leading medical journals, using Bayesian methods. We included 169 primary outcomes from 130 negative trials (p-values > 0.05) across various medical fields, and 234 outcomes from 225 positive trials (p-value < 0.05) in oncology. We used uninformative priors for illustration, supplementing them with skeptical priors in sensitivity analyses. We estimated the probabilities that active treatments were more effective or safe than controls, for each outcome. We also estimated probabilities that the treatment effects were above specific thresholds for clinical significance. We described three of the included trials in more detail and additionally analyzed one trial in neurology as didactical case studies, to illustrate the use of probabilistic statements. Results So-called negative studies may sometimes yield clinically relevant evidence of an effect: in 26/169 (15%) cases we found > 90% probability that the experimental treatment is better than control; for 12/169 (7%) of them, this probability was > 95%. Conversely, positive trials may not always show evidence of clinically meaningful effects: in 25/234 (11%) of the positive oncology trials, there was less than 50% probability that treatment reduces hazards by 20% or more. Our case studies illustrate how to use probabilistic statements in medical decision making in practice. Conclusions Relying on statistical significance without considering clinical importance can mislead decision-making and potentially harm patients. Probabilistic statements from Bayesian analyses can complement traditional approaches to communicating clinical trial results.

title: Co-exposure to CO2 and heatwaves and the risk for diabetes: a multi-center spatial epidemiological study in China
abstract: Climate change, closely linked to the increasing CO 2 concentrations and heatwave events, may directly and indirectly affect the risk for diabetes, which has been a leading cause of disability worldwide. Using the baseline survey of a large multi-center cohort including 134,403 participants in China, this study for the first time examined the associations of CO 2 and heatwaves with the risks for diabetes/prediabetes at an individual level. The exposure to CO 2 and heatwaves was estimated at spatial resolutions of 10 km and 27 km, respectively. Multilevel logistic regression models with random intercepts at the community level were used to estimate the associations after adjusting for individual-level covariates. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses investigated the variations and robustness of the association, respectively, while mediation analysis estimated the mediation effect of body mass index (BMI) on the association. Elevated fasting blood glucose levels were associated with higher CO 2 concentrations ( β = 0.09 [95% CI: 0.07, 0.12]) and increased heatwave frequency ( β = 0.22 [95% CI: 0.09, 0.35]), both of which were also associated with the increased risks for diabetes (CO 2 : OR = 1.14 [1.09, 1.19]; heatwaves: OR = 1.48 [1.17, 1.89]). The association between CO 2 and diabetes was stronger among individuals with less than a high school education, those residing in rural areas, and those living in non-compact built environment. The association between heatwaves and diabetes was stronger among individuals consuming ≥ 400 g/day of fruit and vegetable. Among those who experienced heatwaves, BMI mediated about 8.2% and 2.9% of the associations between CO 2 and diabetes and prediabetes, respectively; among those who did not experience heatwaves, BMI mediated about 11.5% of the association between CO 2 and prediabetes. Higher CO 2 concentrations and increased heatwave frequency were associated with a higher risk of diabetes in China, with BMI partially mediating CO 2 -diabetes association among individuals who experienced heatwave events. This study would advance our understanding of the health effects of climate change and provide scientific evidence for climate change mitigation.

title: Perspectives and challenges for delivering spinal cord injury research and exercise interventions during inpatient rehabilitation in the UK
abstract: Abstract Background The subacute period following spinal cord injury (SCI) is an important window for rehabilitation and exercise research, yet delivering clinical trials during inpatient rehabilitation within the UK National Health Service (NHS) is challenging. Fragmented care pathways, limited specialist capacity, workforce and bed pressures, complex governance, and variable clinical practice can restrict recruitment, intervention delivery, and follow-up. Main body Drawing on experiences from three recent UK inpatient exercise-intervention trials, relevant SCI rehabilitation literature, and perspectives from senior rehabilitation clinicians, we examine barriers and opportunities for delivering research during subacute SCI rehabilitation. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) and RE-AIM framework are used to consider factors affecting research reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. Key challenges include delayed access to specialist rehabilitation, patient readiness and consent burden, competing clinical and therapy priorities, limited protected research time, variable research infrastructure across centres, and difficulties retaining participants following discharge. Greater integration of research and clinical care may be supported by patient-centred and staged recruitment, earlier clinician involvement in study design, protected research time, more coordinated research infrastructure and governance, pragmatic and flexible trial designs, and hybrid delivery incorporating inpatient, remote, or home-based components. Conclusion Subacute SCI rehabilitation provides an important opportunity for evidence to improve long-term care, but current NHS structures can make such research difficult to deliver. Embedding research more closely within routine rehabilitation, while aligning study procedures with patient priorities and clinical realities, may improve feasibility, participation, and translation into practice.

title: Symptom-based clustering of post-COVID patients and its association with healthcare utilisation and long-term health outcomes: a multicentre cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Although the incidence of SARS‑CoV‑2 infections has declined, post‑COVID remains a major public health challenge. Individuals with post‑COVID experience multisystem symptoms and prolonged functional impairment, placing a burden on both affected individuals and healthcare systems. Symptom‑based clustering may identify more homogeneous subgroups and support efficient and appropriate care. This study aimed to identify symptom‑based clusters among individuals with post‑COVID and to examine associations with healthcare utilisation and long‑term health outcomes. Methods This multicentre cohort study included adults (≥ 18 years) with persistent symptoms following SARS‑CoV‑2 infection who were referred to post‑COVID outpatient clinics at three hospitals in the Netherlands. Symptom‑based clusters were identified using K‑means clustering based on reported post‑COVID symptoms at the initial visit. After a mean follow‑up of 2.5 years, all participants were invited to complete a digital questionnaire assessing current health status and quality-of-life. Patient characteristics, post‑COVID symptoms, healthcare utilisation, and long‑term health outcomes were described across clusters. Results Among the 1,155 patients in this cohort (67% female; median age 50 years; median time since infection 24.1 weeks), four symptom‑based clusters were identified. The Respiratory‑dominant & Dyspnoea cluster (47.7%) comprised 47.7% of the cohort, followed by the Fatigue‑dominant & Neurocognitive cluster (27.6%), the Fatigue‑dominant & Multisystem cluster (12.7%), and the Respiratory‑dominant & Airway‑Systemic cluster (11.9%). Patients in the fatigue‑dominant clusters were more frequently referred to occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, mental health services, or a rehabilitation programme than those in the respiratory‑dominant clusters (all p < 0.01), who more often received pharmacological treatment. At 2.5‑year follow‑up, the fatigue‑dominant clusters continued to show a higher disease burden, as reflected by worse PROM outcomes compared with the respiratory‑dominated clusters. Notably, anxiety and depression scores increased over time in all clusters. Conclusions This study shows that, despite the heterogeneity of the post‑COVID population, distinct symptom‑based groups can be identified. Clusters dominated by fatigue were characterised by higher healthcare utilisation and poorer long-term health outcomes. Notably, only 12% belonged to the group with predominant systemic symptoms. These findings may contribute to more tailored management strategies based on patients’ symptom profiles, thereby supporting effective care planning and earlier access to appropriate interventions.

title: The cardiovascular–liver–metabolic syndemic and mortality and life expectancy: two prospective cohort studies
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD), metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and obesity frequently coexist and share overlapping pathophysiologic mechanisms, collectively constituting a cardiovascular–liver–metabolic (CLM) syndemic. However, the mortality and life expectancy consequences of their co-occurrence remain insufficiently quantified. We included 429,722 UK Biobank and 38,759 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) participants. CLM burden was defined as the number of coexisting conditions among CVD, MASLD, T2DM, and obesity (range 0–4), and the CLM syndemic as the co-occurrence of all four conditions. Cox proportional hazards and Fine–Gray models were used to assess associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality, respectively. Life expectancy was estimated using age-specific survival models and expressed as years of life lost relative to participants with no CLM conditions. During median follow-ups of 13.7 years (UK Biobank) and 9.5 years (NHANES), mortality increased stepwise with higher CLM burden. Relative to participants with no CLM conditions, the fully adjusted HRs for all-cause mortality increased with CLM burden, from 1.55 (95% CI 1.51–1.59) for one condition to 2.26 (95% CI 2.18–2.34) for three conditions in the UK Biobank, and from 1.27 (95% CI 1.11–1.47) to 1.90 (95% CI 1.63–2.20) in NHANES. The CLM syndemic was associated with the highest risk of all-cause mortality (UK Biobank: HR 3.58 [95% CI 3.42–3.74]; NHANES: HR 3.10 [95% CI 2.59–3.72]), with the strongest association for CVD mortality (UK Biobank: sHR 8.39 [95% CI 7.51–9.38]; NHANES: sHR 3.88 [95% CI 3.04–4.95]). At age 50 years, life expectancy decreased from 36.9 to 30.0 years in the UK Biobank and from 34.3 to 24.8 years in NHANES. The CLM syndemic was associated with 6.9 (95% CI 6.6–7.2) and 9.5 (95% CI 8.2–10.6) fewer years of life expectancy, respectively. Across two large cohorts, the CLM syndemic was consistently associated with the highest mortality risk, particularly cardiovascular death, and with substantial reductions in life expectancy. These findings support integrated cardiovascular, liver, and metabolic prevention and care strategies to reduce premature mortality and preserve life-years.

title: Healthcare workers and caregivers’ perspectives on access to cancer screening for people with intellectual disabilities as revealed by system dynamics and group model building
abstract: People with intellectual disability (ID) face multiple barriers that limit their participation in cancer screening. This study applies a system dynamics approach, using group model building, to identify factors that influence cancer screening for people with ID and to explore how interconnections shape participation. Group model building workshops were conducted with healthcare professionals and support workers involved in caring for people with ID in the Netherlands. Participants mapped key variables and their interconnectedness influencing access to, and participation in, cancer screening for people with ID during the sessions. And during causal loop diagram assessment an independent group of similar participants validated the developed causal loop diagram. The workshop discussions were used to further interpret and contextualize the diagram. The causal loop diagram captures the central factors affecting cancer screening participation by people with ID. Rather than presenting isolated barriers, the model comprises of 48 variables visualizing the dynamic interactions within the broader system. The model identifies five interconnected thematic clusters representing the decision-making trajectory: (1) awareness of the screening invitation, (2) understanding information, (3) well-informed decision making, (4) access to participation, and (5) system-level visibility and oversight. A key finding is the critical role of the decision-making moments in the screening process, underscoring the need for a multidisciplinary approach to enhance participation. This study enhances the current literature by providing a deeper, system-level understanding of how interacting factors influence cancer screening among people with ID. Beyond the need for accessible information and accessible procedures, continuous support for decision‑making across different stages of the screening process and among involved stakeholders is essential to improve access to screening participation.

title: Close but unreachable: racial disparities in hospice utilization beyond geographic proximity among older adult patients with cancer
abstract: Hospice care reduces the use of aggressive care at the end-of-life; however, not everyone receives this supportive care. This study examines patterns in the relationship between hospice availability and hospice care utilization among Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with poor-prognosis cancer in the United States during 2018. We analyzed this association while accounting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, driving distance to hospice, rurality, neighborhood income, and neighborhood racial composition using a logistic mixed-effect regression model. We also stratified analyses by race/ethnic sub-groups and distance ranges from a hospice. We found that beneficiaries who were female, older, and lived in urban ZIP codes had higher odds of hospice enrollment than their counterparts. In contrast, Black, Hispanic, or Asian beneficiaries had lower odds of hospice use than White beneficiaries. Contextual factors, including neighborhood income and racial composition, showed statistically significant interactions with beneficiary race, indicating heterogeneous effects across groups. In contrast, proximity to hospice did not demonstrate meaningful effect modification across other predictors in stratified analyses. These findings suggest that geographic proximity alone does not fully explain patterns of hospice utilization. Rather, hospice use is shaped by interacting structural and sociodemographic factors that vary across populations. Our results highlight the need for a pathway-based model grounded in systems thinking that captures how, when, and through what interactions multiple factors emerge and influence hospice decision-making over time. Such an approach may provide clearer intervention targets and better explain persistent disparities in hospice utilization among Black, Hispanic, and Asian patients at the end-of-life. Female, older, and urban beneficiaries had higher odds of enrolling in hospice. Black, Hispanic, and Asian patients had lower odds of hospice use than White beneficiaries. Geographic proximity to hospice alone is an insufficient measure of hospice access. A systems thinking approach can help identify gaps and structural barriers in decision-making for hospice enrollment.

title: Segmentation of high-cost patients in England: insights from a machine learning analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Segmentation of high-cost patients can be used to inform service design. We aimed to cluster high-cost patients in the English healthcare system into distinct groups based on diagnoses and socioeconomic characteristics. Methods We examined primary and secondary care costs in the financial year 2018/19 for 10,119,490 adult patients registered with general practices in England contributing to the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and linked to Hospital Episode Statistics, representing around 23% of the adult population in England. High-cost patients were defined as those in the top 1% of total care costs. We used multiple unsupervised machine learning approaches to group patients based on diagnoses, age, sex, deprivation, and ethnicity, and evaluated the resulting clusters for validity and stability using established indices. We also examined several patient subgroups, including age-stratified groups, in-year decedents and patients with the highest unplanned care costs. Results High-cost patients accounted for 26.8% of total healthcare costs in the study population. They had average annual costs of £17,485 (median: £14,609; interquartile range: £12,028£19,633, 2018 prices) compared with £653 (median: £103, interquartile range: £14–£352) for the population. The optimal clustering method was hierarchical clustering, which produced nine clusters with distinct multimorbidity and sociodemographic profiles. Across those clusters, mean age varied between 56 and 79 years and mean annual costs per cluster ranged between £15,792 (95% CI: £15,629–£15,955) and £19,107 (95%CI: £18,784–£19,430). Several core clinical profiles recurred across different clustering approaches and subgroup analyses, including younger people with liver disease and mental health conditions, patients with nodal metastases, patients with prostate cancer and nodal metastases, and older people with cardiovascular disease and dementia. Conclusions High-cost patients are a heterogeneous population with distinct clinical and sociodemographic profiles and utilisation patterns. Incorporating cluster-based approaches into population health management may help inform the targeting of case management programmes, resource allocation, and health system planning.

title: Multimodal neuroimaging of cue-induced craving and cortical alterations in etomidate use disorder
abstract: Despite the escalating global abuse of etomidate, a GABA A -specific anesthetic, the neurobiological mechanisms underlying craving and structural brain alterations remain poorly understood. This case-control study aimed to identify the neural characteristics of cue-induced craving and cortical brain changes in etomidate use disorder (EUD). Right-hand males aged 18–45 years meeting DSM-5 criteria for EUD and age-matched healthy males for controls (HC) were recruited in Guangzhou, China, between June 2023 and October 2024. Within a cue-reactivity paradigm, spatiotemporal neural dynamics of drug craving were investigated using multimodal neuroimaging, including electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in independent cohorts. Effective connectivity was analyzed with dynamic causal modeling (DCM), and structural MRI (sMRI) was further employed to assess cortical thickness. EEG analyses demonstrated amplified frontocentral late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes in response to drug cues in the EUD group, which correlated with subjective craving. FMRI analyses revealed cue-induced hyperactivation in the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC). Signed cue-modulated DCM parameters indicated abnormal VLPFC-to-TPJ inhibitory modulation in the EUD group, with weaker inhibitory modulation associated with higher subjective craving. Furthermore, sMRI identified widespread cortical thinning across prefrontal, parietal, occipitotemporal, and limbic regions among EUD individuals. These findings suggest that chronic etomidate exposure is associated with altered VLPFC function, maladaptive top-down inhibition within the VLPFC-TPJ connectivity, and heightened salience attribution to drug cues. These findings highlight the VLPFC-TPJ circuit as a promising neuromodulation target for treating EUD, underscoring its clinical potential in addressing this growing public health issue.

title: The LIP score: a pathophysiology-driven tool for sepsis screening and prognosis—a multicenter prospective study
abstract: The development of convenient and effective screening tools for sepsis is a critical global priority, yet a systematically evaluated and efficient tool for early identification remains lacking. In this prospective, multicenter observational study across 10 tertiary hospitals in China, the novel LIP score (Lymphocyte count, INR, Procalcitonin) was validated against established tools. Analytical methods included ROC curve analysis for performance comparison, Restricted Cubic Splines (RCS) for ICU length of stay (ICU-LOS) association, and advanced visualizations (Sankey/Chord diagrams, SHAP) for risk stratification and feature interpretation. Among 1,202 enrolled adults with suspected infection, the LIP score demonstrated superior performance. For sepsis diagnosis (cutoff ≥ 3), its AUROC was 0.932 (95% CI: 0.916–0.945), with a sensitivity of 85.37% and a specificity of 94.83%, significantly outperforming all comparator scores (all P < 0.001). In mortality prediction, LIP surpassed SIRS ( P < 0.001) but was inferior to NEWS ( P = 0.031) and SOFA ( P < 0.001), while comparable to qSOFA ( P = 0.28). LIP scores showed a biphasic relationship with ICU stay and modestly predicted microbiological confirmation, on par with qSOFA, APACHE-II, and NEWS. As an early-warning tool, a threshold of LIP ≥ 2 provided high sensitivity (94.58%) but limited specificity (62.72%). Notably, applying a modified rule (any two of three components ≥ 1 point) increased the specificity to 83.14%. This multicenter study validates the LIP score as a simple and efficient screening tool for sepsis in hospitalized patients, demonstrating good diagnostic performance at a cutoff of ≥ 3 and close association with clinical outcomes; preliminary data also suggest promise for emergency use, though further validation is needed.

title: Hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy plus lenvatinib and programmed death receptor 1 inhibitor for hepatocellular carcinoma with portal vein tumor thrombosis: a prospective controlled study
abstract: Lenvatinib plus programmed death receptor 1 (PD-1) inhibitor had shown efficacy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with macrovascular invasion, and hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) had shown promising efficacy for HCC with portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT). This trial was to compare the efficacy and safety of HAIC combined with Lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitor to Lenvatinib plus PD-1 inhibitor for advanced HCC with PVTT. In this open-label, single-center, prospective controlled study, participants with treatment-naïve advanced HCC and PVTT were enrolled from December 2021 to December 2023 and assigned to receive either HAIC combined with Lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitor (Lenva-PD1-HAIC group) or Lenvatinib plus PD-1 inhibitor (Lenva-PD1 group). The primary endpoint was six-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate. Overall survival (OS), PFS, objective response rate (ORR) per mRECIST criteria, time to progression (TTP), and safety were also investigated. A total of 66 participants were enrolled, with 33 in each group. The 6-month PFS rate was 78.8% vs. 46.9% (cloglog P = 0.013). Median PFS (13.7 vs. 5.9 months, hazard ratio [HR]: 0.422, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.229 – 0.778, log-rank P = 0.004), OS (25.4 vs. 12.6 months, HR: 0.502, 95% CI: 0.273 – 0.926, log-rank P = 0.024), and TTP (15.1 vs. 6.2 months, HR: 0.345, 95% CI: 0.170 – 0.700, log-rank P = 0.002) were longer than those in the Lenva-PD1 group, with the ORR per mRECIST criteria of 78.8% vs. 42.4% ( P = 0.003). Sensitivity analysis using propensity score overlap weighting yielded treatment effect estimates that were generally similar in both direction and magnitude with the primary findings. The incidence of Grade 3 – 4 treatment-related adverse events in the Lenva-PD1-HAIC and Lenva-PD1 groups was 57.6% vs. 42.4%. HAIC combined with Lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitor was associated with improved efficacy and acceptable safety profile for advanced HCC with PVTT compared to Lenvatinib plus PD-1 inhibitor. Sensitivity analyses yielded generally similar treatment effect estimates, and confirmation in larger randomized studies is warranted. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05166239).

title: Not all light exposure measures are equal: a framework for exposure assessment and causal inference in light epidemiology
abstract: Abstract Background Light exposure is increasingly recognised as a modifiable environmental determinant of human health. Large-scale studies using satellite-derived outdoor light, wrist-worn sensors, bedroom illuminance meters and other scalable exposure measures have reported associations between daily light-dark patterns and psychiatric, metabolic, cardiovascular, sleep-related and mortality outcomes. These findings have increased the visibility of light exposure within population health research and have provided evidence at scales that cannot be achieved in laboratory or small field studies. At the same time, they raise a foundational exposure-science question: what light exposure construct is being measured and how closely does that construct correspond to the biologically relevant stimulus at the eye and retina? Main body In this Debate , we argue that the next phase of light epidemiology requires a construct-centred framework for exposure assessment. Satellite-derived night-time radiance, wrist-worn illuminance, bedroom light, corneal-plane light, retinal exposure after optical and pupillary modulation and modelled circadian stimulus are related but non-equivalent constructs. Each may be appropriate for particular scientific questions, but each supports different forms of inference. The central challenge is therefore not whether scalable proxies should be used, but how their meaning, uncertainty and relationship to ocular exposure can be specified and empirically quantified. We propose a forward-looking framework for population light exposure research based on explicit definition of exposure constructs, validation across measurement sites and spatial scales and pre-specified causal models linking behavioural determinants, 24-hour light exposure, biological pathways, intermediate phenotypes and clinical outcomes. Conclusions This framework is intended to support the integration of high-throughput epidemiology with physiologically interpretable measurement, enabling the field to move from broad associations towards mechanistically informed and translationally useful evidence.

title: Prevention and management of bleeding complications in interventional ultrasound: an international expert consensus statement
abstract: Interventional ultrasound has become an essential minimally invasive modality in modern medicine, encompassing biopsy, drainage, sclerotherapy, and ablation. With the growing complexity of procedures and expanding clinical indications, bleeding complications have emerged as a critical concern, potentially compromising treatment outcomes and posing life-threatening risks in severe cases. However, no systematic international consensus exists on the prevention and management of these complications. This international expert consensus statement was developed by a multidisciplinary panel of 51 specialists from six countries. The development process followed the World Health Organization Handbook for Guideline Development, was reported in accordance with the Reporting Items for Practice Guidelines in Healthcare statement, and was appraised using the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II instrument. Evidence quality was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach, and recommendations were refined through a two-round modified Delphi process. A total of 20 recommendations were finalized, covering classification, risk assessment, periprocedural prevention, post-procedural monitoring, and stepwise management of bleeding complications. A dual classification based on time of onset and severity is proposed to support standardized clinical communication and decision-making. Multidimensional pre-procedural risk assessment incorporates procedural risk, patient-related factors, lesion characteristics, device-related factors, and operator experience. The recommendations also address individualized periprocedural management, risk-adapted post-procedural ultrasound surveillance, and stepwise hemostatic management ranging from local compression and tract embolization to selected ultrasound-guided interventions, transarterial embolization, and surgery. These recommendations provide a practical framework for clinical decision-making across a broad range of interventional ultrasound procedures while allowing individualized application according to procedural characteristics, patient-related risk factors, operator experience, and institutional resources. The available evidence remains heterogeneous across procedures, and some recommendations are partly dependent on expert opinion where high-quality direct evidence is limited. This consensus statement provides a standardized, evidence-based framework to guide clinical practice, improve patient safety, and optimize procedural outcomes in interventional ultrasound. Further multicenter prospective studies are needed to validate and refine these recommendations.

title: Left atrial appendage occlusion versus oral anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: Abstract Background Data comparing left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) with contemporary oral anticoagulation (OAC) remain uncertain, particularly in the era of safer and more effective direct oral anticoagulants. We investigated the comparative safety and efficacy of LAAO and OAC in patients with atrial fibrillation. Methods We conducted a systematic literature search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane from January 2000 to April 2026, to identify eligible randomized controlled trials comparing LAAO to OAC in patients with atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were ischemic stroke, major and non-major bleeding, and systemic embolism. Pooled effect sizes were calculated using fixed or random effects models and expressed as risk ratios (RR) or mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence intervals. Results Six RCTs comprising 7004 patients (LAAO: 3681; OAC: 3323) were included. There was no statistically significant difference in all-cause mortality between groups (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.87-1.22, p = 0.65; I²=0.0%). LAAO was associated with a significantly higher risk of ischemic stroke compared to OAC (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.04-1.68, p = 0.03; I²=0%). Non-major bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAO (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.43-0.58, p = 0.002; I²=0%) with no statistical difference in the major bleeding outcome (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.73-1.16, p = 0.38; I²=0%). We found no significant difference between groups in terms of systemic embolism (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.41-4.07, p = 0.60; I²=0%). Conclusions LAAO was associated with a significantly higher ischemic stroke risk, while reducing non-major bleeding, however with no significant reduction in the major bleeding outcome overall. Additionally, groups were comparable in terms of all-cause mortality, and systemic embolism. These findings support a cautious, individualized approach to LAAO adoption in clinical practice.

title: Cord blood metabolic network profiles link prenatal rare earth element exposure to neurodevelopmental delay in 2-year-old children
abstract: Prenatal exposure to rare earth elements (REEs) has been linked to impaired neurodevelopment in children; however, the underlying biological mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. In the Wuhan Healthy Baby Cohort ( N = 1,045), we quantified thirteen REEs in first-trimester maternal urine and conducted metabolomic profiling of cord blood. Cognitive neurodevelopment was assessed by the Bayley Scales of Infant Development at 2 years of age. Overall mixture effects of REEs were evaluated using quantile g-computation (qgcomp) and weighted quantile sum (WQS) regression. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was used to identify key metabolic modules and further examine their mediating role in the associations between REE exposure and neurodevelopmental outcomes. After covariate adjustment, each one-unit increase in natural log-transformed maternal urinary concentrations of seven REEs (neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, holmium, erbium, thulium and ytterbium) was significantly associated with higher odds of cognitive developmental delays (CDD), with adjusted ORs ranging from 1.13 to 1.25 ( P < 0.05). WQS regression revealed positive mixture effects of REEs on both CDD and psychomotor developmental delays, identifying ytterbium and cerium as the primary contributors to each outcome, respectively. We applied WGCNA to cord blood metabolomic data using a soft-thresholding power of 5 (scale-free R 2 = 0.87) and identified 13 color-coded metabolic modules. Prenatal REE exposure was associated with perturbations in modules enriched in lysophospholipids and phosphatidylethanolamines, and mediation analyses further demonstrated that these two modules partially mediated the associations between REE exposure and increased risk of neurodevelopmental delay. Prenatal REE exposure is associated with neurodevelopmental delay in children, partly through disruption of phospholipid metabolism. These findings highlight the need for health risk assessment of REE exposure during pregnancy and provide clues for potential intervention targets.

title: Delirium and subsequent psychiatric disorders in hospitalised older adults
abstract: Abstract Background Delirium is an acute confusional state and a frequent and potentially preventable complication of hospital admission. It is frequently accompanied by agitation and hallucinations reflecting physiological stress on the brain, and may precipitate psychiatric disorders in vulnerable individuals. We examined whether in-hospital delirium is associated with new-onset psychiatric disorders. Methods We conducted a matched cohort study using UK Biobank inpatient records from England, Scotland, and Wales (1997–2022), with follow-up up to 26 years. Adults with a first ICD-10 coded hospital episode of delirium (n = 14,909) were matched 1:1 to controls without recorded delirium on age, sex, Hospital Frailty Risk Score, primary diagnosis, length of stay, and ICU admission. Prespecified incident psychotic, bipolar, depressive, and anxiety disorders were identified from inpatient ICD‑10 codes. Personality disorders served as a negative-control. Associations were estimated as subdistribution hazard ratios (SHRs) from Fine–Gray models adjusted for competing risk of death, socioeconomic factors, and polygenic risk scores for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Results Among 29,818 participants (mean age 72.1 years; 57% men), incidence of any psychiatric disorder was 4.9 per 100 person-years in hospitalised participants without delirium and 6.7 per 100 person-years with delirium. Delirium was associated with a 44% higher incidence of any psychiatric disorder (SHR 1.44, 95% CI 1.31–1.59). Risk was greatest for psychotic disorders (3.79, 2.63–5.45) and bipolar disorders (3.44, 1.90–6.20), followed by depressive (1.52, 1.36–1.70) and anxiety (1.37, 1.22–1.54) disorders. No association was found for personality disorders. Only psychotic disorders showed a dose-response relationship with recurrent delirium: each additional delirium episode within 12 months conferred 23% higher risk (1.23, 1.09–1.39). Conclusions In-hospital delirium is associated with increased long-term incidence of psychiatric disorders, with psychotic disorders showing a particularly strong and dose-dependent association. Delirium might represent a potentially modifiable risk factor for subsequent mental illness that warrants further investigation.

title: Glymphatic dysfunction predicts drooling severity in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Drooling (Sialorrhea) is a prevalent and burdensome non-motor symptom in Parkinson’s disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. The glymphatic system is implicated in the clearance of pathological α-synuclein, and its dysfunction may contribute to PD progression. This study aimed to investigate glymphatic system alterations in PD patients with drooling and their links to clinical biomarkers. We enrolled 72 PD patients, subdivided into 36 with drooling (PD-DR) and 36 without drooling (PD-NDR), alongside 38 age-matched healthy controls (HC). All participants underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and clinical assessments evaluated disease severity and drooling using standardized scales. MRI parameters, including the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS), choroid plexus volume (CPV), and enlarged perivascular spaces (EPVS), were calculated. The PD-DR group showed significantly lower left ALPS-index (ALPS_L), right ALPS-index (ALPS_R), and average of the bilateral ALPS index (ALPS_BA) than the PD-NDR ( p = 0.032; p = 0.004; p = 0.004) and HC groups ( p < 0.001 for each comparison). Additionally, the PD-DR and PD-NDR groups exhibited significantly higher CPV relative to the total intracranial volume (CPV/TIV) compared to the HC group ( p < 0.001; p = 0.006). No significant differences were observed in EPVS/TIV among the PD-DR, PD-NDR, and HC groups (all p > 0.05). Lower ALPS indices correlated with greater disease severity and more severe drooling symptoms in both the PD-DR and PD groups. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis demonstrated that ALPS_BA best differentiated PD-DR from PD-NDR with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.725. The multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that ALPS_BA was identified as an independent predictor for the occurrence of drooling in PD (OR and 95% CI, 0.063 [0.004–0.938], p = 0.045) Our findings may indirectly provide in vivo evidence of more pronounced glymphatic dysfunction in PD patients who exhibit drooling. The ALPS index correlates with symptom severity and may show promise as a novel imaging biomarker for predicting the occurrence and progression of drooling in PD, offering new insights into its pathophysiology.

title: Human–AI interaction in parotid ultrasound diagnosis: a prospective two-phase observer-performance study
abstract: Differentiating pleomorphic adenoma (PA) from Warthin’s tumor (WT) — the two most common benign parotid neoplasms — on ultrasound is challenging even for experienced ultrasonographers. Most existing AI systems for parotid ultrasound have been static, retrospective, and tested without prospective reader evaluation. We developed a confidence-aware AI system with a radiologist-editable interface and prospectively evaluated its impact on radiologist performance in an observer-performance study. We developed a confidence-aware hybrid pipeline combining a YOLO detection model with a classification model fallback for parotid ultrasound differentiation, using an internal dataset of 949 images (Korea University Ansan Hospital) and an external dataset of 427 images (Korea University Anam Hospital). We exploratorily evaluated 35 detection × classification combinations to characterize model complementarity, and then prospectively validated a single pre-specified deployment configuration (τ = 0.80, YOLOv12m + ConvNeXt) through a two-phase observer-performance study with three board-certified radiologists on 107 external cases (321 reads total). Standalone detection and classification models achieved external AUROCs of 0.811 and 0.919, respectively. The confidence-aware pipeline outperformed both standalone models in 22 of 35 combinations on external data (highest macro-F1 = 0.838) with the complementary effect most apparent when the two models performed comparably. In the reader study, AI assistance improved pooled diagnostic accuracy from 76.3% to 81.6% (generalized linear mixed model [GLMM] odds ratio = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12–2.13, p = 0.008) and inter-reader agreement (Fleiss’ κ increasing from 0.475 to 0.611), with larger gains on more difficult cases. Reader response was selective: readers followed correct AI predictions more often than incorrect ones (76.2% vs. 51.1%, p = 0.008), and per-class sensitivity changed in opposite directions for WT (+ 18.1% points) and PA (− 9.3% points), aligning with the AI’s prediction profile. A confidence-aware AI system with a radiologist-editable interface improved radiologist diagnostic accuracy and inter-reader agreement in a prospective observer-performance study. These findings support the system’s potential as a decision-support tool that operates alongside the interpreting physician, and motivate further evaluation in real-world clinical workflows.

title: Revisiting brain asymmetry in schizophrenia: insights from machine learning subtypes from 1,761 patients
abstract: Brain asymmetry serves as a measure of typical neurodevelopment, and its disruption is implicated in the etiological framework of schizophrenia (SZ). While previous studies have reported significant alterations in brain structural asymmetry in SZ patients, their interpretations are often limited by relatively small sample sizes, varying approaches to process MRI data, and inconsistent findings. This study aims to identify robust brain asymmetry alterations in SZ using large-scale neuroimaging data, and to investigate how these alterations vary across neuroanatomical subtypes. We analyzed T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from 1,761 individuals with SZ and 1,513 healthy controls (HC), primarily of East Asian ancestry. Regional asymmetry in cortical thickness, surface area, and subcortical volume was quantified using a standardized pipeline. We examined case-control differences in regional asymmetry and further compared two neuroanatomical subtypes previously derived using a machine learning algorithm (i.e., Subtype and Stage Inference). Compared with HC, SZ patients displayed significantly reduced leftward asymmetry in the rostral middle frontal gyrus, reduced rightward asymmetry in the medial orbitofrontal cortex, and enhanced rightward asymmetry in the amygdala ( p < 0.001, Bonferroni-corrected). Comparison with prior Western cohort findings over 5,000 SZ individuals revealed only moderate similarity in cortical surface area asymmetry ( r = 0.36, p = 0.02), with no significant correlations for cortical thickness or subcortical volume. Subtype differences emerged in temporal and parietal lobes, precentral gyrus, and caudate ( p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected). Furthermore, asymmetry in anterior cingulate volume correlated differently with negative symptoms across subtypes (permutation test, p < 0.05). This study confirms that while case-control asymmetry effect sizes are small, they are statistically significant in certain regions when SZ is stratified into neuroanatomical subtypes. These findings extend the long-standing hypothesis of abnormal cerebral asymmetry in SZ, and underscore the influence of subtype and ancestry on observed asymmetry alterations.

title: Age, period, and cohort effects in the population-level incidence and mortality of cancer types associated with early onset increases in Australia
abstract: The incidence of early-onset cancers has increased in recent decades, with hypothesised inter-generational changes in overlapping environmental and behavioural risk factors implicated in changing trends. This descriptive-analytic study investigates the age, period, and cohort effects in population-level incidence and mortality of cancer types previously associated with early onset increases in the Australian population, compared to selected cancer types without early-onset increases. Age-period-cohort modelling examined whether there were differences in temporal trends in Australian cancer incidence (1982–2021) and mortality (1971–2023) between cancer types with early onset increases (breast, colorectum, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreas, thyroid, prostate, oesophagus) and comparator cancers (lung, cervix, melanoma of the skin). For early onset cancer incidence, there was an increasing cohort effect for both males and females in colorectal, liver, pancreatic, thyroid cancers, and for uterine cancers among women, and for prostate cancer among men. The largest relative increase was in pancreatic cancer among females, and thyroid cancer among males. Decreasing cohort effects were evident for melanoma of the skin and cervical cancer (among women), with no substantial differences across birth cohorts for lung cancer and oesophageal cancer. Period effects (adjusting for cohort effects) were relatively stable, except for prostate cancer for males and cervical cancer for females. Decreasing period and cohort effects for cancer mortality were evident for most cancers and for both males and females. The exceptions were an increasing period effect for thyroid cancer and pancreatic cancer, and cervical cancer and uterine cancer (for females). This study found higher population-level incidence of cancer types associated with early onset increases among later born cohorts, which may indicate cohort-specific differences in risk factors associated with these outcomes.

title: Chinese consensus on the management of pancreatic portal hypertension
abstract: Pancreatic portal hypertension (PPH) is a distinct type of portal hypertension caused by various pancreatic diseases or surgery. In recent years, the detection rate of PPH has steadily increased with the widespread application of advanced imaging techniques and endoscopy. Its clinical manifestations are often insidious, compromising early identification. Notably, some complications, such as splenomegaly and upper gastrointestinal bleeding, frequently occur at advanced stage of PPH. Although the concept of PPH has been recognized in existing guidelines and/or consensus on the management of pancreatic diseases or portal hypertension, its management strategy has not been comprehensively summarized. Accordingly, the Chinese Society of Gastroenterology of the Chinese Medical Association invited a panel of skilled experts to participate in the Delphi consensus by systematically reviewing and discussing the available evidence on the causes, risk factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, therapy, and prognostic assessment of PPH. After three rounds of questionnaire surveys and votes, 19 consensus statements were formulated to provide the clinical guidance on the diagnosis and management of PPH.

title: ‘People need to be a bit more understanding that my body is wrecked’: A qualitative exploration of inpatient hospital care for people living with multiple long-term conditions
authors: on behalf of the ADMISSION Research Collaborative
abstract: Abstract Background Living with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC) is becoming increasingly common with far-reaching consequences for individuals and healthcare systems. People with MLTC often face complex care pathways through health systems - especially hospitals, which are largely configured for specialist treatment of single conditions - yet evidence on people with MLTC’s lived experience in the hospital setting is limited. This study aimed to understand the hospital care experiences of people living with MLTC who had recently had an inpatient stay. Methods People with MLTC who had experienced an inpatient stay in hospital within the previous six months were recruited via three hospitals in England and via patient networks. Semi-structured one-to-one interviews were conducted with each participant, focussing on their experiences of care from admission to discharge. An inductive thematic analysis was undertaken. Results A total of 44 people (mean age 68.4 years, 23 women) who reported living with between 2 and 11 long-term conditions, the majority of whom (96%) reported that their most recent hospital stay was unplanned, participated in the study. Three themes were constructed from the interview data, reflecting perceptions at individual, interpersonal and organisational levels. Participants’ experiences were shaped by internalised narratives of hospital care , where care was expected to be focussed primarily on single conditions within a resource-constrained environment. Relationally, the degree of alignment between clinician and patient knowledge on conditions was a key contributor to whether hospital care was experienced positively or negatively, and participants’ perceptions of organisational constraints to holistic care gave insights into their views on system-level barriers shaping the provision of care for MLTC in the hospital setting. Conclusions Experiences of inpatient hospital care for people with MLTC are complex, diverse and shaped by expectations of care in a specialist setting configured to provide care for single conditions. Healthcare professionals should incorporate patients’ experiential expertise into decision-making processes through consultation with people with lived experience of MLTC. Redesigning hospital services to provide holistic care will require flexibility to respond to the wide spectrum of MLTC experiences.

title: Front-line decision-making: a thematic analysis of interviews with hospital staff on referrals, admissions, and care for people with multiple long-term conditions
authors: on behalf of the ADMISSION Research
abstract: Abstract Background Multiple long-term conditions (MLTC) are increasingly common and present challenges for hospital healthcare professionals (HCPs) making decisions about admissions, referrals, and care management in the context of a single-organ oriented health system. This qualitative study examined how HCPs in emergency and acute hospital settings make such decisions for people living with MLTC, exploring factors that influence clinical judgement and how HCPs respond to these challenges. Methods HCPs involved in making decisions about care for people living with MLTC presenting to hospital were recruited via National Health Service (NHS) research delivery networks and professional contacts, using purposive and snowball sampling. Semi-structured individual interviews were conducted, focusing on how HCPs make decisions regarding the care of people living with MLTC and factors influencing such decisions. Reflexive thematic analysis was undertaken. Themes relating to influences on decision-making were organised using the Social Ecological Model (SEM). Results We interviewed 40 HCPs working in NHS emergency departments and acute assessment units across multiple regions, specialties and roles. Seven themes were constructed and organised into two overarching categories. The first category ‘Factors Influencing Decision-Making’ included the themes the complex patient , professional expertise and identity , system pressures and inflexible structures . These themes were mapped to the SEM, demonstrating influences across individual and environmental levels. The second category ‘Adaptive Decision-Making Strategies’ included the themes Mitigating risk and Relying on heuristics capturing how HCPs navigate the uncertainty created by these influences. The theme, Relational care , operated between categories, illustrating how relationships both shape what decisions are possible (interpersonal level of SEM) and provide a means of navigating uncertainty. Conclusions Clinical decision-making for people living with MLTC in emergency and acute settings is shaped by uncertainty arising from the interaction of factors operating across individual, interpersonal and environmental levels. To manage this uncertainty, staff employ a range of adaptive strategies. However, participants described this level of compensatory work as challenging and potentially insufficient on its own. Supporting decision-making and reducing reliance on adaptive responses may benefit from system‑level change, including improved community care, enhanced generalist expertise, opportunities for relational decision-making, better continuity and shared ownership of care, and flexible care pathways.

title: Networked control of bone homeostasis: interfacing post-translational modifications with cellular signaling
abstract: Bone homeostasis depends on the coordinated activity of osteoblasts, osteoclasts, osteocytes, and its microenvironment.
