This prospective cohort analysis included 188,405 UK Biobank participants with Oxford WebQ dietary data. A study-specific UPF-like food-group index comprised processed meat, sweet snacks, savoury snacks, sweet-tasting beverages and ready/fried foods. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) per 1-standard-deviation higher score for incident type 2 diabetes and cardiometabolic multimorbidity, with sequential adjustment for demographic factors, conventional nutrients, body mass index and a nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) biomarker score. Median follow-up was 14.4 years for type 2 diabetes and 14.3 years for cardiometabolic multimorbidity. The total index was associated with type 2 diabetes in the base model (HR 1.20, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.17–1.22) and cardiometabolic multimorbidity (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.11–1.15). After nutrient adjustment, corresponding HRs were 1.18 (95% CI 1.15–1.20) and 1.11 (95% CI 1.09–1.13); after adding body mass index, 1.09 (95% CI 1.06–1.11) and 1.06 (95% CI 1.04–1.08). Additional NMR adjustment yielded HRs of 1.07 (95% CI 1.05–1.10) and 1.05 (95% CI 1.03–1.07). In nutrient- and body-mass-index-adjusted models, the sweet-tasting beverage subtype composite was associated with type 2 diabetes (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.10–1.15) and cardiometabolic multimorbidity (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.07–1.10). Savoury snacks showed smaller positive associations. The minimally processed plant-food minus UPF-like difference index was inversely associated with both outcomes (type 2 diabetes HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.90–0.94; cardiometabolic multimorbidity HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.93–0.96). Although the overall UPF-like dietary index was associated with incident type 2 diabetes and cardiometabolic multimorbidity, the observed associations appeared to be driven primarily by sweet-tasting beverages and, to a lesser extent, savoury snacks, with considerably weaker evidence for the remaining food groups. Reporting component food groups alongside UPF-related indices may distinguish food-specific associations from broader dietary patterns for understanding cardiometabolic risk.

title: Pattern-specific plasma proteomic responses to alcohol drinking and gastrointestinal disease risk
abstract: Alcohol-related gastrointestinal risks vary by intake level, beverage type, and sex, but reported alcohol intake may not fully reflect biological responses to drinking. We aimed to characterize plasma proteomic responses to distinct drinking patterns, assess their associations with gastrointestinal risk states, and identify shared proteins of alcohol exposure. We analyzed plasma proteomic data from 47,514 UK Biobank participants. Drinking patterns were defined by intake level, dominant beverage type, and sex, yielding 12 pattern-specific proteomic signatures. Linear and nonlinear associations with gastrointestinal disease risks were evaluated. Shared alcohol-responsive proteins were examined and validated in an independent cohort and a graded ethanol-exposure mouse model. Alcohol drinking was associated with 475 plasma proteins enriched in immune, inflammatory, adhesion, and lipid-related pathways. Alcohol-related proteomic responses were highly pattern-specific, differing by intake level, beverage type, and sex in the composition, pathway enrichment, and overlap of signature proteins. Pattern-specific proteomic signatures showed heterogeneous and nonlinear associations with gastrointestinal outcomes. Even among drinkers with similar alcohol intake levels, beverage- and sex-specific signatures displayed distinct risk curves for the same outcomes, suggesting that alcohol-related proteomic responses capture information beyond alcohol volume alone. Despite this heterogeneity, APOM, MAMDC4, and SERPINA7 were consistently retained across drinking patterns, correlated with alcohol intake, discriminated regular drinkers from occasional drinkers better than conventional liver enzymes, and were validated in the Chinese cohort and ethanol-exposed mice. Distinct alcohol drinking patterns were characterized by different plasma proteomic response states, which provided biological context for heterogeneous gastrointestinal disease risks beyond reported alcohol volume alone. APOM, MAMDC4, and SERPINA7 represent shared exposure-responsive proteins that may complement questionnaire-based alcohol assessment.

title: Recommendations for managing multiple long-term conditions: a systemaftic guideline review and modified Delphi study
abstract: Recommendations for managing multiple long-term conditions (MLTC) aim to support healthcare professionals in delivering patient-centred, goal-oriented and coordinated care. Previous systematic reviews and consensus studies have informed MLTC management, and new guidance has become available since. However, challenges persist in implementing recommendations into routine clinical practice. Establishing consensus on the relevance of recommendations is an important prerequisite for subsequent evaluation of the feasibility and priority for implementation. Therefore, we conducted a systematic guideline review to identify recommendations and used these in a modified Delphi study with international experts to reach consensus on key recommendations for the management of MLTC. A systematic guideline review was performed to extract all recommendations on the management of MLTC. Using a snowball recruitment approach, we identified 53 professional experts on MLTC from 25 countries who agreed to participate in two online Delphi survey rounds to assess recommendations most relevant for the management of MLTC. Agreement for inclusion was defined a priori as ≥70% of respondents rating a recommendation ≥7 on an 11-point numeric rating scale (0 not important and 10 extremely important). Open-ended questions allowed for comments and additions. A total of 297 recommendations were extracted from 14 guidelines and synthesized into 65 recommendations to be assessed in the modified Delphi procedure. Forty-two experts (response rate 78%) reached consensus on the relevance of 32 recommendations in the first round. In the second round, 40 experts (response rate 74%) re-evaluated eleven recommendations derived from the first round and assessed four recommendations newly formulated based on open-ended responses. In this round consensus was reached on five recommendations in total, resulting in 37 consensus-based recommendations. As a final step, we refined these 37 recommendations into a final list of 31 across six categories: 1) approach to care addressing MLTC, 2) comprehensive assessment, 3) patient-centred consultation, 4) individualized care plan, 5) monitoring and follow-up, and 6) collaboration and coordination. The key recommendations represent a broadly endorsed set of advice, supporting healthcare professionals and policymakers in designing strategies to improve the quality of care for patients with MLTC.

title: Factors associated with the use of UK emergency services in children and young people with intellectual developmental disabilities
authors: Marianne B. M. van den Bree
abstract: Abstract Background Children and young people (CYP) with intellectual developmental disabilities (IDD) experience substantial health needs and higher healthcare utilisation compared with the general paediatric population. However, factors affecting the emergency healthcare use among children with IDD of genetic aetiology remain poorly understood. This study aimed to examine demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, genetic, and clinical factors of emergency service use among CYP with IDD in England. Methods This retrospective cohort study used linked administrative healthcare data from Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) emergency service records obtained from National Health Service (NHS) England. Participants were CYP aged between 4 and 15.5 years with confirmed pathogenic genetic variants associated with IDD identified via NHS medical genetic clinics. The outcome was the yearly emergency service use rate, calculated as the total number of lifetime emergency visits divided by age (years). Independent variables included demographic and socioeconomic factors, genetic characteristics, region of residence, adaptive functioning, behavioural and emotional adjustment, prosocial behaviour, general health status, and system-specific medical conditions. Primary caregivers completed questionnaires and provided information regarding the child’s medical history and demographic information. Results The average emergency attendance rate in this cohort was 0.73 visits per annum, which was much higher than that among children in the same age range from the general population. Emergency services were used more by younger IDD children with poorer adaptive functioning, more externalising and less prosocial behaviour, as well as those with complex multisystem conditions. Frequent attendance was associated with high rates of medical comorbidities especially seizures and respiratory problems. Regional differences were found with relatively higher usage in London and the North East of England. Attendance rates were not influenced by sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, genetic variant type or inheritance status. Conclusions This novel study demonstrated emergency healthcare utilisation among CYP with IDD of known genetic aetiology in England was primarily associated with clinical complexity, functional impairment, and younger age rather than socioeconomic or genetic factors. Their vulnerability to multisystem morbidity as well as regional disparities highlight the need for improved coordinated care and targeted service planning to reduce emergency healthcare dependence among children with disabilities.

title: Associations between neuropsychiatric symptoms and cerebrospinal fluid amyloid pathology, and convergent proteomic signatures in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Abstract Background Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPSs) are highly prevalent in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and may accelerate cognitive decline, but the molecular mechanisms linking NPSs to AD pathology remain unclear. Methods In this cross–sectional study, we analyzed 713 Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants with available NPSs assessments, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) amyloid–β42 (Aβ42), SomaScan 7 K proteomics, and cognition data. NPSs were assessed using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire and clustered into four subsyndromes (hyperactivity, psychosis, affective, and apathy). Associations between NPSs, CSF Aβ42, and cognition were examined using regression and mediation analyses. Weighted gene co–expression network analysis (WGCNA), protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, and Mendelian randomization (MR) were applied to identify and validate NPSs–associated protein modules and hub proteins. Results Higher NPSs burden, as well as hyperactivity, affective and apathy, was cross-sectionally associated with lower CSF Aβ42, which partially mediated the NPSs–cognition association. WGCNA identified three NPSs–associated modules. MEyellow, the largest and most phenotypically relevant, was enriched in protein folding, ubiquitination, stress responses, and immune regulation, predominantly in neurons. PPI network analysis revealed a hub cluster centered on the heat shock proteins (HSP) and ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes E2 families, which significantly mediated the NPSs–Aβ42 association. MR supported causal effects of HSPB1 on hyperactivity and HSPA1A on apathy. Conclusions These findings suggest a potential relationship among NPSs, reduced CSF Aβ42, and cognitive impairment, and implicate the HSP family as a candidate therapeutic target for early intervention in AD, pending further validation.

title: Remote monitoring for gestational diabetes: neonatal and maternal outcomes compared to usual care
abstract: Digital care is increasingly used to alleviate capacity use in hospital care. This pre-post study assesses the effect of remote monitoring compared to usual care in a large cohort of women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). We assessed large for gestational age (LGA) newborns, caesarean sections, pregnancy-related maternal and neonatal complications, and hospital service use. Two independent groups of women treated for GDM in a large teaching hospital in the Netherlands were compared: a group from January 2020 until November 2022 receiving usual care, and a group between December 2022 and February 2025, predominantly receiving remote monitoring (intervention). Routine antenatal care was provided in parallel. The usual care group received GDM care according to hospital guidelines. The intervention group received remote monitoring by default, with glucose measurements transmitted via an application and monitored by Virtual Care Centre nurses. Data was collected on demographical and clinical characteristics, LGA, complications, hospital service use, and remote monitoring aspects. A non-inferiority margin of 8% points was set for LGA. In total, 623 patients with GDM were included. In the intervention group 81% received remote monitoring. LGA was present in 20.3% of newborns in the remote monitoring group and 17.8% in the usual care group (estimated difference 2.5% (95% CI: -3.9 to 9.0%)). The upper-bound of 9% exceeded the pre-specified 8% non-inferiority margin, and thus results are inconclusive. No significant differences in complication rates were found. The mean number of outpatient clinic visits per patient during pregnancy for the internal medicine department was 1.6 ± 1.2 for the remote monitoring group, and 2.8 ± 1.9 for the usual care group ( p <.001). Adherence to glucose measurements was good. Most patients did not need Virtual Care Centre nurse interventions and most messages sent to patients were automatically generated. No statistically significant difference in LGA proportions was observed between groups, however sample sizes were insufficient to establish non-inferiority. Remote monitoring did not affect caesarean sections and pregnancy-related maternal and neonatal complication rates. Hospital service use was reduced. Further research on subjective experiences and clinical outcomes of GDM may contribute to optimizing remote monitoring and reducing capacity use.

title: Proteomic profiling of acute postprandial responses to five single-meal challenges and implications for cardiometabolic health
abstract: Diet influences human health, but the acute molecular effects of individual meals remain incompletely understood. In this prospective crossover study, 20 healthy volunteers underwent five single-meal challenges: high-glucose/OGTT, ketogenic, high-fat high-calorie (HFHC), normal-fat normal-calorie (NFNC), and low-fat low-calorie (LFLC). We collected 500 plasma and 500 urine samples and performed high-throughput proteomic profiling. Mendelian randomization was used to assess the genetic relevance of diet-responsive proteins to cardiometabolic outcomes. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04984642). Each meal induced a distinct proteomic response. Compared with LFLC, the ketogenic meal increased PPBP, SRGN, GSTO1, BLVRB, MIF, and S100A4, implicating platelet activation, inflammation, and oxidative-stress-related processes. Compared with the high-glucose challenge, HFHC altered JUP, DSP, APOA5, TAGLN2, RAP1B, and TMSB4X, involving cell adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, lipid transport, and endothelial-related pathways. The high-glucose challenge reduced PRDX1, CAT, and SOD1, suggesting acute perturbation of redox-defense pathways. Exploratory urinary proteomic analyses showed complementary meal-specific responses, including enrichment of hydrogen peroxide catabolism and cellular oxidant detoxification. Participants with overweight/obesity had higher baseline CRP, LILRA3, and SERPINE1, lower ADIPOQ, and altered postprandial protein-triglyceride associations, including distinct APOA5- and PGM1-triglyceride correlations after HFHC. Single meals induced acute, diet-specific plasma and urinary proteomic responses involving pathways relevant to inflammation, oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, platelet activation, and vascular function. These findings provide mechanistic insights into potential links between meal composition and cardiometabolic health. The publicly available postprandial plasma and urine proteomics dataset provides a valuable resource for studying how daily eating may influence health.

title: BigpictureQC: multi-stain, multi-species artifact segmentation for whole-slide quality control
abstract: Abstract Background Artifacts in digital pathology whole-slide images (WSIs) cause diagnostic delay and quality issues, yet quality control (QC) in most pathology laboratories remains manual, subjective, and difficult to scale. We present BigpictureQC, a deep learning framework for WSI quality assessment based on per-class pixel-level segmentation of six visually distinct artifact and marking classes. Methods BigpictureQC was trained on 268 WSIs from five data sources and evaluated on >9,200 WSIs spanning human and preclinical samples, diverse tissue types, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and immunohistochemical (IHC) stains, and multiple scanner models. Patch-level segmentation was evaluated on 569 WSIs from seven independent cohorts using the Dice similarity coefficient for pixel-level segmentation; slide-level artifact detection was assessed on an independent dataset of 315 dermatopathology WSIs using F1 scores. A quantitative slide-level quality score was derived from artifact coverage and evaluated against manual quality ratings using Spearman rank correlation and AUC. Clinical impact was evaluated in a retrospective cohort of 3,686 diagnostic slides with technician rescan decisions and a prospective cohort of 4,426 unreviewed slides from routine diagnostics. Results BigpictureQC achieved a mean Dice score of 0.93 on the evaluation set, outperforming academic and commercial baselines across all artifact classes and domains (H&E, IHC, clinical, preclinical). Slide-level artifact detection yielded a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.93. The derived quality score strongly correlated with manual ratings and achieved an AUC of 0.978 for identifying poor-quality slides. In clinical workflow analyses, automated quality control identified 93% of poor-quality slides, compared with 35% detected by routine manual inspection. In the prospective-style cohort, 8.2% of slides were identified as having substantial quality issues that would otherwise have reached pathologists without prior review. Conclusions BigpictureQC provides the first publicly available automated QC framework validated across human and preclinical digital pathology, encompassing multiple tissue types, H&E and IHC stains, and diverse scanner models. It substantially outperforms existing manual and automated approaches in detecting poor-quality slides, and demonstrates strong potential to improve laboratory efficiency by enabling systematic pre-screening of all digitized slides at the point of scanning. The code, inference pipeline and trained model weights are publicly released.

title: Polygenic and classical risk integration reshapes breast cancer screening recommendations in 9,761 Asian women
abstract: BACKGROUND: Age-based mammography screening fails to account for individual breast cancer risk variation, particularly in Asian populations where prospective evidence is absent. METHODS: The BREAst Screening Tailored for HEr (BREATHE) study is a multicentre prospective cohort of 4,513 women aged 35-59 years recruited across six Singapore clinical sites (2021-2023). Risk-stratified screening recommendations were assigned using a five-year absolute risk threshold of 0.9% (equivalent to the population-average risk of an average 50-year-old Singaporean woman) to initiate screening based on polygenic risk score (PRS) and Gail model, as well as mammographic density, family history, abnormal prior screening. Two independent breast cancer case cohorts provided comparative analyses: Singapore Breast Cancer Cohort (SGBCC, n = 2,782) and Malaysian Breast Cancer Genetic Study (MyBrCa, n = 2,466); combined n = 9,761. RESULTS: Among 2,003 healthy women aged 40-49 years currently recommended annual mammography, risk stratification downgraded 776 (38.7%) to no screening and 960 (47.9%) to biennial as they were not in the top 2.5th percentile of PRS and Gail risk and did not have any additional risk indicators. Of 41 breast cancers diagnosed after BREATHE enrolment, 35 (85.4%) occurred in women assigned to screening-eligible categories at baseline. Risk stratification combining PRS and Gail model captured 68-69% of cases aged 40-49 in SGBCC (n = 1,184) and MyBrCa (n = 1,122), versus ~ 54% by PRS alone. Relative to cases meeting screening criteria for both PRS and Gail model, PRS-missed cases were enriched for progesterone receptor negativity (OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.01-1.52), tumour size ≥ 50 mm (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.02-2.00), and germline protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in breast cancer predisposition genes (OR 1.53; 95% CI 1.03-2.29). CONCLUSIONS: Risk stratification combining PRS with classical risk factors reshapes mammography recommendations in Asian women. However, due to the limited number of events in BREATHE, this finding requires evaluation in larger prospective studies. PRS-missed cancers exhibit a biologically aggressive profile, defining the current limits of common-variant prediction and identifying the biology that future precision screening tools must address.

title: Mindfulness meditation plus transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for alcohol use disorder: a randomized clinical trial
abstract: Abstract Background Impaired inhibitory control under negative affect is a core mechanism sustaining alcohol use disorder (AUD), but receives limited attention in treatment development. Mindfulness meditation has shown efficacy in improving this function, but outcomes differ across individuals. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a noninvasive neuromodulation approach that targets brain–heart interplay. It may enhance neurobiological pathways underlying emotion regulation and cognitive control and thus represents a promising augmentation strategy. This randomized controlled trial examined whether concurrent taVNS augments the efficacy of mindfulness meditation on inhibitory control under negative affect and whether brain–heart interplay represents a relevant physiological pathway. Methods Sixty-three patients with AUD were randomized to receive either sham ( n = 31) or active ( n = 32) taVNS during twice-daily mindfulness meditation sessions for 10 days. Inhibitory control under negative affect was measured by no-go accuracy when angry faces were presented as distractors in a color-based go/no-go task. Tonic brain–heart interplay was quantified by heart rate variability-electroencephalography coupling at rest. Secondary outcomes include latency to any post-discharge alcohol use, craving, negative affect, emotion regulation, mindfulness, and sleep quality. Primary analyses used ANCOVA to predict post-treatment angry-face no-go accuracy from group and baseline. Additional analyses examined changes in brain–heart interplay indices and self-reported outcomes across groups. Results Mindfulness meditation with active taVNS produced greater increases in angry-face no-go accuracy than mindfulness meditation with sham taVNS ( p < 0.001). Post-treatment accuracy remained baseline-dependent in the sham group (β = 0.406; 95% CI, 0.245–0.567; p < 0.001), whereas the active group achieved uniformly high accuracy regardless of baseline (β = -0.015; 95% CI, -0.205–0.175; p = 0.798). Enhanced BHI occurred only in the active group. Reductions in anxiety and craving were greater and earlier in the active group than in the sham group. Conclusions The combination of mindfulness meditation and taVNS provides an effective and safe treatment for men with AUD. The results support the promise of targeting brain–heart interplay to develop interventions for AUD. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07036055. Registered on June 16, 2025.

title: The association of risk factors, circulatory biomarkers and antihypertensive medications with preeclampsia: a Mendelian randomisation analysis
abstract: Abstract Background While many risk factors for pre-eclampsia (PE) have been identified, their causal role and the potential preventive effects of specific antihypertensive drug classes remain unclear. Methods We examined the potential causal effect of 22 risk factors and two genetically proxied antihypertensive drugs (Beta-blockers and Calcium channel blockers) on PE development and its two related conditions, PE-HTP (PE or other maternal hypertension) and PE-SGA (PE or delivery of a small for gestational age neonate). Using summary statistics from published genome-wide association studies, we employed two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) using Wald ratio or inverse variance weighted. MR Egger, weighted median and MR-PRESSO (Pleiotropy RESidual Sum and Outlier), Multivariable MR (MVMR) and Bayesian colocalization analyses were performed where appropriate. Results Maternal body mass index (BMI), systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP) were significantly associated with all PE outcomes. Higher BMI was associated with increased risk of PE (Odds ratio (OR) = 1.50, P = 1.58 × 10⁻⁸), PE-HTP (OR = 1.72, P = 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁷) and PE-SGA (OR = 1.35, P = 2.06 × 10⁻⁵). Elevated SBP showed strong associations with PE (OR = 2.74, P = 3.90 × 10⁻²⁶), PE-HTP (OR = 3.64, P = 4.23 × 10⁻³⁷) and PE-SGA (OR = 2.21, P = 5.01 × 10⁻¹⁸). Increased DBP was significantly linked to PE (OR = 2.33, P = 7.03 × 10⁻¹⁷), PE-HTP (OR = 3.08, P = 9.59 × 10⁻²⁷) and PE-SGA (OR = 2.04, P = 8.38 × 10⁻¹⁴). Age at menarche was associated with PE-HTP, but this effect was mediated by BMI. Genetically proxied calcium channel blockers (CCB) were linked to with lower odds of PE and PE-HTP in the DBP-based drug-target MR (OR per SD reduction = 0.31, P = 0.001 and OR per SD reduction = 0.17, P = 5.12 × 10 − 6 , respectively), with consistent findings observed in the complementary SBP-based analysis. Conclusions The findings validate the significant role of cardiovascular factors in the PE pathogenesis and highlight new therapeutic possibilities.

title: Type 2 diabetes and obesity: integrated strategies for managing atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk
abstract: Abstract Background Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality among individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D). Despite effective low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) reduction and optimal management of conventional risk factors, individuals with T2D continue to have significant residual ASCVD risk. Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] and triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnants are increasingly recognised as key drivers of this residual risk. Moreover, the interplay between T2D and obesity accelerates atherosclerosis through multiple interconnected mechanisms. This review highlights the evolving landscape of ASCVD management in individuals with T2D, with and without obesity, focusing on advances in cardiovascular risk prediction, emerging biomarkers, novel pharmacological therapies and non-pharmacological strategies. Main Text Advances in cardiovascular risk prediction have improved risk stratification among individuals with T2D. Diabetes-specific risk models, together with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven approaches, enable the integration of multimodal data beyond traditional risk factors, providing more robust cardiovascular risk assessment. Pharmacological developments have facilitated a shift towards precision-based management through targeting specific atherogenic pathways. Emerging treatments targeting Lp(a), triglyceride regulation, and gene-editing technologies have expanded the therapeutic landscape in ASCVD management. In parallel, organ-protective therapies have transformed the management of T2D and its complications. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA)-based therapies have demonstrated significant cardiovascular-kidney benefits, together with clinically meaningful weight reduction, independent of glycaemic control. Beyond pharmacological interventions, effective public health strategies remain essential for reducing cardiovascular burden. Sustained lifestyle modification, environmental interventions, and policy-driven initiatives play important roles in promoting cardiovascular health at both individual and community levels. Conclusions ASCVD prevention in individuals with T2D and obesity is evolving toward a precision-based approach through advanced risk prediction, novel biomarkers, targeted pharmacotherapies, and population-level interventions. These combined strategies are essential to reduce residual cardiovascular risk and improve long-term cardiovascular outcomes.

title: Global clinical development of transcranial temporal interference stimulation: an analysis of registered human trials
abstract: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) is a noninvasive approach intended to engage deep or distributed brain targets. Despite a growing number of human studies, the global landscape, design characteristics, and reporting practices of registered tTIS trials remain unclear. We characterized the global clinical development of tTIS by examining registration trends, trial design, intervention reporting, and result availability. We searched nine international and regional clinical trial registries through April 30, 2026, to identify human interventional trials involving tTIS or related transcranial interferential stimulation approaches. Eligible records were deduplicated and coded for geography, indication, intended target, enrollment, design, stimulation parameters, device or platform information, safety reporting, and result availability. From 1,548 records, 168 unique trials were included. Registrations increased markedly after 2023 and were concentrated in China (79.8%) and the United States (11.3%). Psychiatric disorders were the leading indication group (39.8%), and target information was not reported in 75 trials (​4​4​.​6%). Among reported targets, subcortical structures predominated. Most trials involved a single center (94.6%), and 51.8% planned to enroll fewer than 50 participants. Randomization, masking, and sham control were reported in 69.6%, 74.4%, and 66.7% of trials, respectively. Among stimulation parameters, session duration was reported most frequently (40.5%). Device or platform information was reported in 12.5% of trials. At the data cutoff, 13 trials (7.7%) were classified as completed or terminated. Results were available for 8 trials (4.8%) from 10 sources. Registered tTIS research is expanding rapidly across diverse indications and intended targets, while clinical development remains at an early stage and intervention reporting remains incomplete. Greater transparency and consistency in trial registration and intervention documentation will enhance comparability across trials, facilitate protocol replication and evidence synthesis, and support the development of a more coherent evidence base for tTIS.

title: Risk factors for renal cell carcinoma: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney malignancy. However, evidence regarding its risk factors has not been systematically synthesized. This umbrella review aimed to summarize the existing evidence and establish an evidence-based framework for interpreting these associations. Up to January 2026, a systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Methodological quality of systematic reviews or meta-analyses (SRs/MAs) was assessed using AMSTAR 2, while the certainty of evidence was evaluated with GRADE and further categorized according to the evidence classification criteria. Through a systematic search and selection process, 44 SRs/MAs were identified, of which 32 were included for data extraction. A total of 84 unique summary effect estimates were extracted and classified into three domains: lifestyle factors, circulating biomarkers, and disease and treatment-related factors. Methodological quality of 32 SRs/MAs by AMSTAR 2 ranged from critically low to moderate. GRADE assessment indicated that most associations were supported by very low quality evidence, with only 7 rated as low (moderate alcohol drinking, HCV infection, obesity, ever smoking, kidney transplantation, heart transplantation and each additional serving/day of vegetable intake). Among the statistically significant exposures, 4 were supported by Class I evidence, whereas 10, 10, and 18 were categorized as Class II, Class III, and Class IV evidence, respectively. Low quality evidence suggests that obesity, HCV infection, ever smoking, and solid organ transplantations (kidney, heart) are associated with an increased risk of RCC, whereas an increased daily intake of vegetables is associated with reduced risk. Notably, low quality evidence indicates that moderate alcohol drinking is linked to a lower risk of RCC, but this finding requires further validation from more large-scale, long-term follow-up studies, even though it has been assigned to Class I evidence. Overall, given the low to very low certainty of the evidence in this umbrella review, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, and further high quality prospective studies are warranted to validate these associations.

title: Early-life parental income mobility and risk of depression and anxiety in adolescence and young adulthood among non-immigrants and second-generation immigrants
abstract: Abstract Background Little is known about the association between early-life income mobility patterns and the subsequent risk of depression/anxiety among immigrant populations. Understanding these associations may help identify persistent low income and declining income as potential risk factors for depression and anxiety in immigrant populations. We aimed to investigate whether parental income mobility patterns during childhood are associated with the risk of depression/anxiety during adolescence and young adulthood among non-immigrants and second-generation immigrants, and whether the association differs by immigrants’ region of origin. Methods Swedish nationwide data on 1,194,015 non-immigrants and 315,793 second-generation immigrants who turned the age of 15 between 2001 and 2020 were used. Income mobility patterns were identified using group-based trajectory modeling based on annual parental income data when the study individuals were aged 0–14. Depression/anxiety was assessed using the National Patient Register (inpatient and outpatient) when the study individuals were aged 15–25. Cox proportional hazard models were used to examine the association between income mobility and depression/anxiety by immigrant status and region of origin. Results Five income mobility patterns were identified. Persistent low income was more common among second-generation immigrants than non-immigrants (32.2% versus 12.2%). Compared with persistent high income, persistent low income and downward mobility were associated with higher hazards of depression/anxiety in most groups. Associations were generally weaker among second-generation immigrants, particularly in those from the Middle East or North Africa (MENA). For persistent low income, adjusted hazard ratios (95% Cis) were 2.35 (2.27–2.43) and 2.23 (2.17–2.29) among non-immigrant males and females, versus 1.28 (0.98–1.66) and 1.29 (1.05–1.58) among their MENA counterparts. Among most second-generation immigrant groups, elevated hazards associated with persistent low income were attenuated or absent with upward low–middle mobility. Conclusions The association between childhood economic disadvantage and later depression/anxiety varied by immigrant background, with weaker relative risks among second-generation immigrants from MENA. Upward mobility from low to middle income was associated with attenuated risk compared to persistent low income and downward mobility among most second-generation immigrant groups, suggesting that a change of childhood economic circumstances may be relevant to later mental health.

title: Multimodal prediction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in locally advanced gastric cancer: a multicenter cohort study
abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is a standard treatment for locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC), but response varies greatly among patients. Existing predictive models often neglect host-related factors such as body composition. This study aimed to develop and validate a multimodal model integrating clinical, tumor radiomics, and body composition features to predict NAC response. A total of 1,568 LAGC patients were analyzed, including 1,150 from six centers for model development and validation, 352 in a real-world incremental cohort, and 66 from two prospective trials (ChiCTR2000030414 and NCT03718624). Radiomic features were extracted from pre-treatment CT scans of tumors and L3-level body composition. Feature selection included statistical testing and LASSO regression. A multimodal ensemble model (NeoGEM) was constructed by integrating clinical and radiomic features. NeoGEM achieved high performance in the training cohort (AUC = 0.888; accuracy = 0.809) and showed comparable discrimination across internal (AUC = 0.870–0.875), external (AUC = 0.859–0.877), and prospective cohorts (AUC = 0.864–0.867). The model demonstrated stable predictive performance across different chemotherapy regimens and treatment cycle subgroups. In the incremental real-world cohort, where radiological rather than pathological response was used, NeoGEM also maintained good discrimination (AUC = 0.840), providing supportive evidence of broader clinical applicability. NeoGEM achieved higher AUCs than the clinical, tumor-only, and body-composition-only models across the validation cohorts examined. NeoGEM score stratification was associated with 5-year OS (35.5% vs. 62.4%) and DFS (21.5% vs. 50.8%) in the low vs. high NeoGEM score groups ( P < 0.001). Exploratory transcriptomic analysis suggested immune-related pathway enrichment and higher infiltration of CD4+, CD8+, and FCGR3A+ cells in tumors from high NeoGEM score patients. NeoGEM showed consistently good discrimination across retrospective, external, and small prospective validation settings, suggesting potential utility for response stratification in patients with LAGC. The integration of body-composition radiomics may improve predictive performance and provide additional host-related biological context.

title: Disease-modifying therapies in managing disability worsening in adult relapsing multiple sclerosis: a population-based longitudinal study using the MSBase registry
abstract: Abstract Background Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) reduce inflammatory activity in relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS), yet their long-term effects on disability worsening, and how these vary by age at treatment initiation in routine clinical practice, remain uncertain. We examined age-dependent associations of DMTs with disability progression across clinically meaningful Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) states, including secondary progressive MS (SPMS), while accounting for latent heterogeneity in progression risk. Methods We analysed longitudinal data from the international MSBase registry, including adults with relapse-onset MS (symptom onset ≥ 18 years), ≥ 12 months of follow-up, and ≥ 2 EDSS scores recorded remote from relapse. Disability progression was defined as transitions between five EDSS-based states: nil/minimal (0–1.5), mild (2.0–2.5), moderate (3.0–3.5), gait disability (≥ 4.0), and SPMS. A continuous-time random-effects multistate model jointly estimated worsening and improvement transitions. Associations of low-efficacy and high-efficacy DMTs versus no treatment were assessed with age-by-treatment interactions. Age-stratified treatment effects were summarised as 5-year percentage inhibition of disability progression (%IDP). Random-effects captured unobserved between-person heterogeneity and identified latent progression subgroups. Results Among 15,425 participants (70.9% female), median follow-up was 9.4 years (IQR 4.7–15.6). Overall, 87.9% received DMTs, with 48.7% initiating high-efficacy and 45.9% initiating low-efficacy therapy. Both DMT classes were associated with more favourable disability trajectories across most transitions, including increased likelihood of improvement. Treatment effects were strongly age-dependent, with greatest benefit in younger adults (18–30 years), attenuation through midlife (30–50 years), and weaker or inconclusive effects after age 50, particularly for transitions to SPMS. In 5-year %IDP analyses, inhibitory effects declined monotonically with age. High-efficacy therapy conferred greater inhibition of disability progression than low-efficacy therapy, with evidence of benefit persisting into older age. Two latent subgroups were identified: a rapid-worsening group (76.1%) and a stable/improving group (23.9%), differing markedly in progression hazards and recovery potential. Conclusions In this large real-world cohort, DMTs were associated with sustained but age-dependent reductions in disability progression. Substantial heterogeneity in progression risk supports personalised treatment strategies, improved risk stratification, and enriched clinical trial design.

title: Colchicine use and cardiovascular event risk in Chinese adults starting urate-lowering therapy: a cohort study
abstract: Low-dose colchicine may reduce recurrent cardiovascular events in secondary prevention, but its real-world effectiveness in primary prevention remains uncertain. To examine the association between colchicine use and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk among Chinese adults initiating urate‑lowering therapy. Using the Beijing Medical Claim Data for Employees (2008–2017), we identified adults without prior CVD who initiated urate-lowering therapy. Colchicine exposure was defined as ≥ 1 dispensing within 30 days of initiation. Propensity score fine stratification weighting was used to balance baseline characteristics. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for CVD and its components, including ischemic heart disease, heart failure, and cerebrovascular disease, with stroke and all-cause mortality as secondary outcomes. After weighting, the study included 6,157 colchicine users and 279,309 non-users initiating urate-lowering therapy (median follow up of 3.05 years). Colchicine was not associated with incident CVD (weighted incidence 1.62 vs. 1.59 per 100 person-years; HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.91 to 1.12). No associations were observed for ischemic heart disease (HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.88 to 1.16), heart failure (HR, 1.17; 95% CI, 0.83 to 1.66), cerebrovascular disease (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.79 to 1.12), and stroke (HR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.79 to 1.17). All-cause mortality was lower among colchicine users (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.86). In this large real-world Chinese cohort initiating urate-lowering therapy, colchicine use was not associated with CVD risk. These findings do not support routine colchicine use for primary cardiovascular prevention at urate-lowering therapy initiation.

title: Within-country ethnic disparities in intimate partner violence against women and associated factors across 37 low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Sustainable Development Goal 10 calls for reducing inequalities, including those associated with ethnicity. However, evidence concerning ethnic disparities in intimate partner violence (IPV) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains limited. This study aims to assess within-country ethnic disparities in IPV against women and to examine factors associated with the observed disparities. This cross-sectional analysis used data from Demographic and Health Surveys conducted between 2010 and 2023 in 37 countries. A total of 295,623 women aged 15 to 49 years were included. We estimated the prevalence of IPV by ethnic groups and calculated the Theil index (TI) to assess relative ethnic inequality within each country. We then conducted Fairlie decomposition to quantify the extent to which measured factors at the household, relationship, and individual levels statistically accounted for observed differences between the constructed high- and low-IPV-prevalence ethnic-group aggregates. Physical, sexual, and psychological IPV prevalence varied substantially across ethnic groups in most countries. The TI was significantly greater than zero in 29 countries for physical IPV, 21 for sexual IPV, and 26 for psychological IPV, indicating statistically significant within-country ethnic disparities. Descriptively, relatively large TI values were observed in several low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Furthermore, partner’s alcohol use and witnessing parental IPV accounted for notable proportions of the observed differences across all three IPV outcomes, with corresponding proportions of 13.6% (12.0–15.3) and 6.3% (5.3–7.3) in physical IPV, 8.0% (6.1–9.9) and 4.6% (3.4–5.7) in sexual IPV, and 38.3% (34.0–42.6) and 17.9% (15.0–20.7) in psychological IPV, respectively. Household decision-making and educational level also played substantial roles in explaining disparities in sexual IPV (10.7% and 7.2%), as did attitudes towards violence in psychological IPV (7.5%). Within-country ethnic disparities in IPV were widespread across the LMICs included in this study, although their magnitude varied across countries and outcomes. Partner’s alcohol use, witnessing parental IPV, household decision-making, women’s education, and attitudes towards violence emerged as important factors linked to the observed differences. These findings highlight ethnicity as an important dimension of within-country inequality in IPV and warrant further research into the context-specific factors underlying these disparities.

title: Therapeutic ultrasound for brain intervention: toward bioeffect-linked acoustic dose control
abstract: Central nervous system disorders remain challenging to treat because the blood–brain barrier restricts therapeutic delivery and deep brain structures are difficult to access. Therapeutic ultrasound offers non-invasive access to intracranial targets and can produce diverse biological effects by varying acoustic exposure and biological mediators. However, these applications have largely been developed and evaluated separately, and the field lacks a shared framework for comparing their biological effects, monitoring strategies and translational maturity. This Review organizes therapeutic brain ultrasound within a shared acoustic parameter space defined by frequency, pressure, pulse structure, skull transmission, biological mediators and tissue state. We examine thermal ablation, histotripsy, blood–brain barrier opening, sonodynamic therapy and neuromodulation, alongside emerging applications in liquid biopsy, glymphatic modulation, sonogenetics and acoustic brain–computer interfaces. Thermal ablation is clinically established for selected indications and uses temperature-based monitoring. Blood–brain barrier opening has demonstrated controllable permeability and enhanced drug delivery, although incremental clinical benefit remains to be established in randomized trials. Intracranial histotripsy remains preclinical. Sonodynamic therapy and neuromodulation have shown feasibility and biological or physiological target engagement, but clinical efficacy has not yet been established consistently across indications. To connect these diverse applications, we propose a bioeffect-linked acoustic dose-control framework that distinguishes three non-equivalent layers: patient-specific estimation of intracranial exposure, intraprocedural monitoring or delivered-dose surrogates, and post-treatment validation of intended biological effects and safety. The relevant readouts range from magnetic resonance thermometry and cavitation emissions to sensitizer-linked pharmacodynamics and electrophysiological responses. We outline modality-specific priorities for dose validation, controlled clinical evaluation and longitudinal safety assessment. A bioeffect-linked framework that connects measured or estimated acoustic exposure to modality-specific biological effects may improve reproducibility and guide the transition toward feedback-governed precision brain intervention.

title: Cross-cultural validity of the Pediatric Symptom Checklist – Youth Report (PSC-Y) in five ​Global ​South countries: Implications for equitable child mental health screening
abstract: Abstract Background Despite a high global burden of mental health disorders in childhood and adolescence, access to adequate care remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries​. Valid and reliable self-report instruments are essential for early identification and equitable care, yet measurement invariance as a prerequisite for valid group comparisons remains understudied. The Pediatric Symptom Checklist (PSC) is a brief, open-access screening tool with practical advantages for global use. This study examined the factor structure and measurement invariance of the 35-item PSC youth self-report (PSC-Y) across five Global South countries. Methods We analyzed baseline data from 5,810 children and adolescents (age 6–18 years) participating in school-based randomized controlled trials in Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda, Haiti, and Pakistan. Using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM), we tested competing models (unidimensional, three-factor, second-order, bifactor). Multi-group CFA examined measurement invariance across countries. Within each of the five countries, we tested invariance across gender and across age groups in each of the three African countries where both primary and secondary students were represented, using school level as a proxy for developmental stage. Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes (MIMIC) models served as sensitivity analyses. Results A strong general factor emerged across all countries (omega hierarchical > 0.90). Configural invariance was supported across countries, but metric invariance failed, with items related to empathy, rule-breaking, and anger expression showing differential functioning. Full metric, scalar, and strict invariance were achieved across gender in all five countries. The Tanzania and Uganda samples demonstrated full invariance across school level as a proxy for age, while Ghana required partial invariance after freeing five items (e.g., empathy, fighting). MIMIC models supported these findings. Conclusions The PSC-Y exhibits a strong general factor across diverse Global South settings, supporting total score use for screening within countries. However, because metric invariance was not established across countries, cross-country comparisons of PSC-Y scores are not methodologically defensible. Within countries, full gender invariance validates direct comparisons between boys and girls. Findings underscore the need for ongoing local validation and cultural contextualization for advancing equitable global mental health research and practice.

title: Motivation in adolescents and caretakers undergoing a weight management program – longitudinal data from the cluster-randomized, motivation-focused STARKIDS trial
abstract: Abstract Background Motivation towards behavior change is an important determinant of long-term weight management. Previous research demonstrates that children’s and adolescents’ motivation can be increased through participation in weight management programs. However, little is known about motivational changes in caretakers of children and adolescents with overweight and obesity despite their recognized role as “agents of change” in pediatric weight management. The study aims to compare motivational changes in caretakers and adolescents between a group receiving a motivation-focused weight management program and a control group. Furthermore, predictors for motivational changes are unknown. Methods This study is a secondary analysis of the cluster-randomized STARKIDS trial. The intervention group received an 18-month motivation-focused weight management program, the control group received optimized treatment-as-usual. Motivation was assessed based on Transtheoretical Model, using the University of Rhode Island Change Assessment-Short, as well as the related parent-perspective version. Each of these instruments contains four subscales: Precontemplation, Contemplation, Action, and Maintenance. Linear mixed models with multiply imputed data were employed to evaluate changes within the subscales between pre- to post-intervention measurements and to compare these changes between the intervention and control group. A multiple linear regression was subsequently used to identify predictors of motivational change. Results Caretakers in the intervention group showed significantly greater changes on Maintenance subscale compared to caretakers in the control group at both T0-T1 and T0-T2 and trends for these changes on Action subscale. No group differences were found in adolescents. Among caregivers in the intervention group, multiple regression analysis for T0-T1 changes on Action subscale identified parent-reported adolescents’ obesity-related quality of life as significant negative predictor for an increase on Action stage. Conclusions This motivation-focused weight management program produced motivational gains at the Maintenance stage, supporting sustained behavioral change. Baseline obesity-related quality of life predicted motivational change, suggesting its value as a clinical marker for tailoring interventional approaches. Future research should explore distinct motivational trajectories to inform more individualized pediatric weight management strategies. Trial registration Preregistered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS) DRKS000228 13 (acknowledged primary register of the World Health Organization) on 27 November 2020 (Universal Trial Number U111112549536).

title: mHealth-based lifestyle intervention for hypertension in community-dwelling adults: a cluster-randomized controlled trial with exploratory multi-omics analyses
Digital health for health outcomes: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials
abstract: Abstract Background Digital health interventions offer unique strengths including wide accessibility, scalability, lower workforce dependence, and potential cost savings. Yet evidence on their effectiveness remains inconsistent, and existing evidence syntheses are fragmented, limiting clinical and policy guidance. This umbrella review aimed to address this gap. Methods We searched six databases from inception to April 2025 for meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials comparing digital health interventions with either inactive controls (eg, usual care, attention placebo or waitlist) or standard therapies (eg, face-to-face treatment). Methodological quality, evidence certainty, and credibility were assessed using AMSTAR 2, GRADE, and evidence classification criteria, respectively. Random-effects reanalyses used HKSJ correction, with effect sizes standardised so positive values indicate benefit. Results We included 232 publications encompassing 1133 unique outcomes across 12 condition categories and 559792 participants. Methodological quality was high in 37%, moderate in 12%, low in 32%, and critically low in 19%. Overall, 53 findings had high-certainty and 84 moderate-certainty evidence. Against inactive controls, telemonitoring reduced systolic blood pressure in hypertension (equivalent Hedges’ g 0.55, 95% CI 0.31–0.78). Other high-certainty findings showed telephone-based interventions reduced diastolic blood pressure (0.17, 0.09–0.24), Internet-based cognitive behavioural therapy reduced depression in insomnia (0.38, 0.23–0.54), and telemedicine reduced weight in type 2 diabetes (0.12, 0.06–0.17). Against standard therapies, specific virtual reality improved upper limb function after stroke (0.23, 0.06–0.40), whereas telemonitoring showed no statistically significant differences in hospitalisation, all-cause mortality, or stroke among patients with pacemakers; synchronous virtual consultations showed no difference in HbA1c in type 2 diabetes; and tele-exercise showed no difference in physical function in knee osteoarthritis. All had high-certainty evidence. Additional moderate-certainty findings concerned stroke, Parkinson’s disease, and musculoskeletal conditions. Surgical, maternal-neonatal, and older adult care outcomes included high and moderate certainty findings. Conclusions Digital health interventions are effective but show no superiority over standard therapies in cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, stroke and Parkinson’s disease, mental health, musculoskeletal conditions, postoperative care, maternal and neonatal health, and care for older adults, though effects vary by outcome. Future work should prioritise standardisation, optimisation and inclusive implementation to realise the equity and resilience potential of digital health. Trial registration PROSPERO, CRD42025645564.
